The text, especially in chapter III, is badly scanned; evident readings have been translated (e.g. 'Maximi' for 'Malimi', 'fortasse ... congruentius' in Vallarsi's admonition, 'necabo' passage completed with 'Ego'). Some places remain uncertain: in chap. I 'utqualicunque solatio litterarum enirem' is read as 'sustinerem/fulcirem' (support); in chap. II 'posterior' presumably stands for 'potentior'; in chap. III 'meritum sanitatis ire' and 'curandum causa non cogeret' are obscure, and the surgical passage ('siM scalpollo damere putroeines', ':he lotus homo perenes cradatur', 'it-. urit') has been read as 'scalpello demere putredines', 'ne totus homo perire cogatur', 'ignis urit'. 'Navigium ... agitantibus gaudet' presumably lacks 'ventis'. Ecclus. 2 is attributed to Solomon in the text. The Greek καῦμα ('heat') is glossed in the text by Latin 'cauma'.

Line 6: the Job citation (Job 21) is given as the text has it and does not match the Vulgate closely; the word before 'sua' is lost ('in Ii... sua', perhaps 'in tribulatione sua'). 'Eorum vias nolunt scire' is odd after the first-person 'nolo'; a singular ('non vult', i.e. God) may be intended. 'cum non negant se torturi' is probably corrupt; rendered as 'morituri' (going to die). 'mala virtutis bono potiare' is corrupt; rendered as 'overcome' (perhaps 'superare'). 'pon- temur' read as 'potiamur/ponamur', rendered 'be raised up'. Various evident scanning errors corrected silently (mediam = medicinam, concienetur = concinit, etc.). Line 7: 'Est inter ea saeculum' rendered as 'For the world is'; 'sessores' read as 'vectores' (passengers); 'sarcinam ... annorum' read as 'armorum' (pack of arms).

Line .8: 'cum perierint maximarum exempla virtutum' is obscure; rendered as a contrary-to-fact sense ('would have perished'); the text may be corrupt. 'potens sum' read for scanned 'putens'. The second Pauline 'quotation' ('As often as I am weak…') is not a biblical text. Line .9: 'loca sita' likely corrupt (perhaps 'loca strata' or 'senta'); rendered '[rugged] places'. 'a praeceptoribus ludorum' read for scanned 'a praeceptormus udorum'. Line .10: 'sub damnis disciplinae' read for 'sudamna'; 'contrarium' in 'contrarium vero inter contraria non trepidare' is uncertain; 'cujus tamen castitate impugnamur' read as 'by which our chastity is assailed'.

Line 11: the second speaker label is printed 'UtER.', evidently a scanning error for 'HIERON.'; rendered 'JEROME' per the glossary. The 'worldly' sayings quoted there are from Seneca (De providentia). 'Primone posses' in line 12 is obscure; rendered as 'Could you have borne the first [trials]', with 'eese succedentibus squalis' read as 'non esse ... aequalis'. The reading is uncertain. Line 13 begins mid-sentence: the opening words of the notice are missing in the text as given.

Marianus: presumably Marianus Victorius, Jerome's earlier editor. 'Quadruplici forma' (fourfold form) and 'fenus' (interest): sense unclear; perhaps an allusion to fourfold restitution. 'Bethsaide porticibus ... ignorat' has no expressed subject; the subject has been supplied as [the water], which is conjectural. 'Ad medicum ... Dominus loquitur' is obscure; perhaps corrupt. 'Si subjectus passus sit esse subjectus' is probably corrupt: the sense seems to be that one meant to rule allowed himself to be subject, and [being meant to rule] has been supplied on that basis. 'Interpellatorem' (interloper) probably refers to the devil. 'Pro vitali ratione' is read as 'for the sake of [luxurious] living', but this is uncertain. 'Viii' has been read as 'vili' (cheap). Agobard's quoted portion is marked in the edition by footnote letters, which have been omitted.

In line 17, 'tanti fuit illum fuisse olim' is obscure; it is rendered literally. The sentence beginning 'Si de coelestibus factus' seems elliptical or corrupt, so the implied comparison is supplied in brackets. 'quasi facti ab ipso anteriores' is uncertain. In line 18, 'Si arcana operatione' is read as 'Sic', and 'quominus ac negligentius' as 'quo minus ac negligentius'. The scanned text has many OCR errors, which are corrected silently where the reading is evident.

'quantum valeret praestare non laus' is evidently corrupt; translated as if 'non laesus' (or 'placatus'), contrasting with 'iratos' (read 'iratus'). 'consiliatii' is unclear (perhaps a corruption of a term for dialecticians); rendered 'counsellors'. 'Non indicant humano sensu' read as 'they do not speak by human sense'. The quotation 'Factum ex muliere, factum ex carne' is given as the text has it (Gal. 4:4 reads 'factum sub lege'); the reference 'Galat. XIV' corrected to Gal. 4, 'Genes. XL' to Gen. 25. 'Jesse filius David' is inverted in the text; translated as David son of Jesse. The sentence on David and the law of the firstborn ('quando hoc utique, aut in qua...') is awkward and possibly corrupt. 'Luc. n' reference for Exod. 13 quotation is as printed (Luke 2:23 cites it).

Several references in the edition are wrong: 'Psal. XI' (Blessed are those who search his testimonies) is Ps. 118 (Vulg.); 'Psal. xxII' is Ps. 22 Vulg.; '7 Cor. XXVIII' is 1 Cor. 2:8; 'We shall all rise but not all be changed' is 1 Cor. 15:51, not 1 Thess. 4; 'Rom. iv' is closer to Rom. 15:4 or 1 Cor. 9:10. 'ab homine virginis' perhaps for 'ab nomine'; rendered 'person'. 'et sanos partus, viperarum progenies obsequantur' seems corrupt; rendered tentatively with a gap. 'strumosis acus' (rendered 'swelling needles') is obscure, probably corrupt (perhaps 'acubus'). 'Hoc autem non est angustum' rendered 'not hard to grasp'.

Line 21: 'lapides damnati monstrantur' is obscure and may be corrupt (perhaps an allusion to the stones that would cry out, Luke 19:40); translated literally. 'cum assistet formido de lapsu' read as 'absistet' (fear of falling will depart); 'assistet' (will be present) contradicts the sense. 'Quid et si miseris fiduciam, ut beatis Deus det?' is obscure, possibly corrupt; translated literally. Line 23: the question is attributed to Matt. 25 at its first citation and to Matt. 21 at the second; the passage is Matt. 21:23. 'bea fateor ipsius nanc' is badly scanned; read as something like 'Ita fateor ipsius nunc', and the sense of this sentence is uncertain. 'Hoc loco plene, ut in omnibus...' is syntactically incomplete or corrupt; translated as it stands. 'profuga omnium' is read as given; the sense is uncertain.

Scanning errors read as evident: 'nesciat' for ',eiciat'; 'venturae aetati' for 'venturas ... ætati'; 'nunc per speculum ... nondum tamen' for 'non per speculum ... non tamen'; 'ipsi, quae sunt' for 'ipse, quae nunt'; 'exemplo' for 'exempto'; marginal letters and page numbers omitted. Citations as printed are off: 'quis scandalizatur' is 2 Cor. 11, 'ex parte scimus' and 'cum venerit quod perfectum' are 1 Cor. 13. In ch. XI the sentence on Peter ('quod illi, etsi apud Dominum fiducia erat...') is syntactically broken; bracketed words supply the apparent sense. 'pseudotypum' is uncertain, rendered 'false figure'. The Revelation quotation repeats 'datae sunt illis singulae stolae', apparently a duplication in the text, translated as it stands. 'cessante merito' taken as 'since merit is lacking'.

Several scanning errors are read as evident: 'Melum' as caelum (or Deum), 'libertatis' (twice) as liberalitatis, 'speciem' as species, 'Icerimus' as diximus, 'temediis' as remediis, 'Mediolaui' as Mediolani (Milan). In CAP. XIII the sentence 'Quousque enim imputatio est ... si quousque non fallit' appears corrupt ('sine line' read as sine fine). The translation of this sentence is tentative. In CAP. XV 'eam sequeretur' is taken in the sense of following the bishop. The closing clause is awkward in the Latin.

Line 30: 'Ecce haec ipsa hominem illum nostrum nosse ... distinguere operationum species' is garbled in the edition; the rendering is tentative. The Virgil quotation is Georgics 2.490; the second-placed worshipper of the gods alludes to Georgics 2.493, and the 'cold blood' to Georgics 2.484. 'ex Syracusia ratione' (perhaps alluding to Archimedes) is obscure, and 'eminerer' is read as 'eminere'. 'ito docente' is read as 'illo docente'. Line 31: 'passionem hominis' may be an error for 'possessionem' ('possession of man'). 'de vitiis innumerabilibus' makes no sense here and is read as 'divitiis' ('riches'). 'collusor inlerpolatores' is read as 'collusores interpolatores', and 'inisse' as 'iisse'. 'interposita altitudinem' is unclear, and the rendering is tentative.

'animus suspecti' is odd and may be corrupt; translated literally as 'the suspect'. 'anhelans attitudinem plagarum' read as 'altitudinem' (depth). 'in 'alitum delectabili disputatione' is garbled; read as 'in tantum' or 'in altum' (so far). The sinner's prohibition alludes to Ps. 49(50):16.

nodes.text: FIRST LETTER.
To a sick friend.
FIRST ADMONITION OF DOMENICO VALLARSI, IN VOLUME XI OF THE WORKS OF ST JEROME.

Erasmus once thought that this [letter] was not far from the style of Tertullian, as far, says Vallarsi, as one may scent it from his fragments: for it is rather affected and somewhat harsh, even if weighty in its thoughts. Others perhaps judge, even more fittingly, that it comes so close to the diction of the following letter, which, as no one now denies, is by St Maximus of Turin, that they still do not ascribe it [to him] with certainty. Though I would not yet dare to pronounce on this matter, I nevertheless lean nearer to their opinion, [and think] that the one who wrote this bore the character of a bishop, since he says of himself right at the beginning that he is occupied by the religious necessity of the Lord's affairs.
SECOND ADMONITION.

Among the spurious works of St Maximus we also place two letters once attributed to St Jerome and published under his name. See in the preface the weight of the reasons which drove us to give this judgement against the opinion of Vallarsi and others. Nothing else remains for us to add, except that we have taken the variants from codex x of Pluteus XIX, parchment, in folio, fifteenth century, page 265, of the Medicean Laurentian Library, and from the Roman edition of the Letters of St Jerome by Peter de Maximo, in the year 1468.

CHAP. I. — Although I know most certainly that your experience does not need the reliefs and oars of another's consolation, since you yourself soothe the pains and hardships of a weak body and the numbness of stiffened limbs by the happiness of a vigorous and ardent mind, and treat and settle them by a physician's reasoning; nevertheless, in adversity a defence, in sickness a remedy, in cares a comfort, in the waves the oar of another's hand is always sought and longed for. For the fruit of a brother's consolation is beyond doubt a part of the greatest cures: and the kindling of words, by the sweetness of those who console, brings relief into weary minds. And if not in the bodily limbs, yet in the recesses and hidden places of the mind it restores a person by spiritual care, and brings in health like a physician, and helps the efforts of exhausted strength under the burden of long afflictions: above all since it is written: A brother helping a brother will be exalted (Prov. 18). For this reason, then, since the religious necessity of the Lord's affairs keeps me so occupied that I am not given the opportunity to brighten your hardships by frequent visits in person, it has pleased me, as you asked, to support by some sort of comfort in letters such long trials of virtue, or rather to visit the good of your health, and to advance a mind founded on Christian virtue to the greatest strength. We who strive to seize the spoil of the heavenly kingdoms and the wealth of an everlasting gift cannot be victors without some conflict. For a virtue that is delicate and ignorant of combat never climbs to the palm-bearing summit of victory, nor does anyone receive the prize for adversities subdued, except one who judges the life of his own body cheaper than victory. For he is not shaken by fear of death, for whom life is born from death: to him it is precious even to shed his blood; it is happiness to fight against unhappiness, it is the highest health to endure bitter wounds; he thinks even the loss of limbs the greatest gain. And, what is the last thing, I will say it: it is glorious to him in the very contest to return his palm-bearing soul to its creditor. For it is better, as reason determines, if what is owed to nature is paid to virtue. All things must be borne, brother, they must all be borne, through which the Lord has willed to test you by very long affliction, and to destine you for great rewards.

CHAP. II. — THE SICK MAN. What mind, with strength now sunk, could bear these inevitable mishaps and the onsets of ruinous calamity, and hostile diseases which, as far as I can see, will die only with the body itself? JEROME. One whom the storm has caught among the waves must now engage with the dangers and fight. And though no one willingly suffers or bears danger, yet under the weight of danger, with necessity compelling, he is hardened. THE SICK MAN. But another anxiety comes upon me which, with doubled griefs, wraps up my senses and, in the manner of biting cares, lays inextricable cares upon me. For it troubles me that it has fallen to me alone to struggle with such trials and in a contest with so stubborn a disease, while I know that others have been corrected with milder blows and have come out victors after a short struggle. Why did the Lord not declare a contest on me as on the rest? Why did he not chastise me as he did the others? JEROME. First of all, being set in so arduous a contest, you should not be thinking of humble things. For lower prizes belong to lower fights. In short, where brave tasks are imposed on the brave, a braver wealth of reward follows the braver man; and therefore the brave man judges it a disgrace to be matched with an inferior. For great is he who has conquered great things; it belongs to the greatest devotion to endure the greatest things, to huge virtue to overcome huge things. For he will surpass the others in eminent merits before the king whom the heat (*kauma*) of wars has most troubled, and whom things overcome have rendered a victor. Finally, in the very conflict there is booty suited to the quality of the contest, rightly destined for the victor. Kings impose burdens on the camp's ranks according to their strength; physicians apply remedies according to the causes. The one who must be treated does not tell the physician by what rule he is to be treated; nor does the soldier choose where he is to be sent, nor the slave with what lash he is to be chastised. For what hangs on the will of a greater is not in the power of the subject. Therefore we, who are ruled by the power above and live amid the manifold miseries of the world to be corrected, have no right, as regards the Lord's power, to choose either the blows or other contests which we might conquer by bearing them: just as it is not for slaves to choose from their masters the kinds of whips. For the license of the one who strikes never hangs on the will of the one who hangs [under the lash]. It belongs to power to correct, to condition to submit. It is the king's to impose the burden, and the soldier's to bear it. Indeed, since nothing unjust is done by the king himself, who, imposing the sweat of war on his legions according to the quality of their strength, sends the brave to brave tasks and orders fitting ones for the lesser, so that neither is the lesser constrained against his own strength by the contest of the more powerful, nor is the latter humbled, with his merits lowered, by the contest of the lesser. And while this is done, so that no one is diminished in another's [task] or indeed succumbs, he wishes all to be victors. Nor is the physician an enemy who strikes to remove danger and to shut out a wound by a wound. Nor is a father's affection hostile if it teaches its children with the embraces of whips. For a father's whips are exercises of harmless love. Therefore, since chastisement is the cause of correcting love, coming down as it does from love, love the physician who strikes, whose blow is the mother of medicine. For love brings forth nothing unloving, so that, having embraced the virtues, the one spiritually cured may enclose the fruit of love. [I,] the Lord, he says, will kill, and I will make alive; I will strike, and I will heal (Deut. 32).

CHAP. III. — THE SICK MAN. But you said: So love strikes? JEROME. Certainly it strikes; lest it be judged unloving, if it does not correct the offender. For since there is never lacking in a person something to be cured, it strikes in order to cure, as are the hands of a physician, which bring health by hurting much, not without the patient's grumbling. In this way we too, under the care of the healer's stroke, amid the very straits of grief, grumble against the Lord as the wounded do against the physician, who are being cured and are in pain. Take up, then, brother, take up the remedy of endurance, by which you may be able to lighten the burden heavy with trials, and to overcome dangers while you suffer them. Let the firm mind comfort and treat the prostrate limbs. Let virtue hold the kingdom within a body made captive by anxieties, so that the soul shut in by dangers may flourish by the freedom of virtue itself, which long ago was ordered by the trumpets of the law to be made ready in various ways for the conflict of temptation, and to be armed, at the very first step of the Lord's service, against hostile calamities. Son, he says, coming to the service of God, stand in justice and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation (Ecclus. 2). Therefore, since temptation is extended for our benefit, it is no wonder if its burning befalls us. As the most blessed Peter warns and said in his letter: Do not wonder at the burning that befalls you, which happens for your testing, lest you fall away among the various waves of the world (1 Pet. 4). The Christian life is shaken and tested by frequent storms, and is nursed and grows by countless pressures. This Solomon, the most blessed and very illustrious prophet, attests and proves: Cling, he says, to the Lord, and endure, that your life may grow at the last (Ecclus. 2). The ship of our life rejoices in tossing winds: it is troubled only by calm. For its course comes to a standstill when the winds cease; it is in peril if it is not tested by perils. For it is uncertain whether one belongs to the Lord whom pressure, the mother of glory, does not purge by winnowing, nourish by pressing, prove by chastising, cure by striking. For since divine love bestows on us blows and various other trials, and, like a physician, applies a remedy from contraries and helps by tormenting: he does not prove himself to belong to the Lord's love who has not deserved to lie under healing blows. But perhaps you say: If God is my lover, why then do my lover's whips sadden me with grievous laceration and trouble me by hurting? If he who loves torments me with the embraces of whips, then a false love is practising hatred; I would rather he hated me, so as not to torment me. No, beware lest he hate you; pray that he deign to love you. For love corrects, but hatred threatens punishment. Love is accustomed to bestow discipline; hatred, by the dictate of sentence, to recite the charge. This hatred is propagated from God onto man from the birth of the human race. And so it is man's doing that God hates or is angry: he hates while he is offended, he is angry while, offended, he is not entreated. For he provokes the Lord to hatred of himself who makes himself hateful by hateful deeds, and disdains to entreat the one offended. Otherwise, God loves man as a craftsman loves his work, but he hates the evil deeds by which the work is pushed towards a fall and driven to ruin. And he who hates evil deeds cannot love the doer of evil deeds: as the most holy Solomon declared: Hateful to God, he says, are the impious man and his impiety (Wisd. 14). Therefore it is better in this world, destined to perish as its years decline, whose old age its setting presses on and swallows up, to endure healing blows out of the Lord's love than to await out of his hatred an incurable stroke and, under the thunderbolt of sentence, to lead a damnable life. It is better, being one who will pass through the physician's hands, to endure even a little torment, than to renounce the physician and incur a punishment that will harass [you] with eternal torturers. Or if you still wonder that our lover's medicine consists in whips, you must also wonder that remedies torment those whom the physician loves, who by harming shuts out what harms. Surely one who seeks to shut out harmful things cannot do harm; and so he cures by harming, so that health, prepared by griefs, may be dearer. For if medicine did not lacerate the one to be healed, the reward of health would always delight in a voluntary wound. If the precious care of cures did not consist of harmful remedies with biting aids, the cause would not drive the patient into grief. And so the cure is accomplished by harmful remedies, so that health, redeemed at the price of grief, may be held dearer and welcome. Therefore one who is to be loved cannot fail to be corrected by some testing; one who is to be corrected cannot fail to be whipped by the lover's lash; one who is to be cured cannot fail to be hurt by the healer's sharpness. Why are you stunned with wonder? One whom fire and iron cure looks for help from dangers. For there are many things that are healed only when struck. There are many whom physicians cannot cure without the knife. Those who, when asked, grant health through various torments often, as the disease demands, give for the sake of a remedy very bitter drinks to those who are not thirsty, which are swallowed not without a wrinkling of the brow. For if you look at the drinker's face, he drinks sad and anxious so that he may live happy and unharmed. O perverse enough, yet reasonable, way of medicine, bringing benefits out of discomforts! A man is pressed to drink what he does not thirst for, though sometimes his remedy is what he thirsts for. For since they sometimes prescribe abstinence from food, they waste the body by an imposed fast, so as to render it restored and very strong out of that very weariness. Sudden wounds which chance has brought in the camps they bathe, bind, stitch, treat; they gladden by saddening, strengthen by wearying, heal by hurting. For while, the skin of the parts being joined over the wound with certain clasps, they put health into it, they promise by comforting a life which they establish by curing. But what we have said is lighter: there are those with whom the remedy is to cut away weakened putrid flesh with the scalpel and to amputate dead parts from a living man; though the one member is cut away not without feeling in the whole body, the man nevertheless consents to his losses so that he may live. With them sometimes, the skin drawn back, the very bones are scraped, so that the whole man may not perish. With them sometimes a festering gathering and a burning swelling is furrowed by the medical knife. With them fire burns in order to cool; powder bites and lacerates in order to heal. What more? Under medical love a man is tormented very much so that he may live very long. See a necessary danger, in which a faithful torment is a benefit. He whom the physician treats is certainly in danger, but he who renounces him perishes too. For to the one, though under torment, life is promised; to the other the hope of living is denied. Therefore, where necessity demands, it is better to be in danger than to perish. It is better to be harmed by discomforts with profit than to perish by refusing discomforts: that is, it is better to be harmed by a remedy than to be unable to be cured.

CHAP. IV. — I say this according to heavenly medicine, and I refer it rather to spiritual care, not only to that which, by a perishing art, is busy with mortal limbs. It is therefore better for us to be reproved and chastised by the Lord, and to be cured under his blow, than to be removed from his medicine as incurable. For God keeps away from his face those whom he sees troubled by the iniquity of an incurable disease, scattered and dispersed through their vices like dust or chaff by the force of a whirlwind, as he himself says in his own voice: Let the wicked depart from me, for I do not wish to know their ways; for their lamp has been put out, and they shall have groaning in their [...]. For they shall be like chaff that flies before the wind, and like dust that is lifted up by storms (Job 21). Their ways they do not wish to know, who do not wish to keep the way that leads to the heights. For to the one Lord one way in Christ must be kept, which through narrowing trials leads into the space of long security. To this way alone the palace of heaven lies open; but the others, twisting with the windings of pleasures, make for the flame-bearing region. Of these Solomon thus testifies in his own voice: There are ways that seem just to men, and at their end are sadness and pain (Prov. 14). And along these ways those men walk headlong whom the course of a hostile life flatters with deceitful allurements; whom deaf time deceives and beguiles, receives for destruction and shuts in. As a storm drives a ship to perish upon the rocks, so an unhappy happiness leads them, prone and slipping, to destruction. And as the smoothness of marble or an upturned slab of pavement, by a sudden fall, has twisted someone walking with secure steps, though his feet were safely set: so those whom the uncertain road of prosperity and a wickedly pleasant life unhappily lead must needs be driven by a sudden fall into an irrecoverable slip, as the most holy Solomon testifies and cries out: As one, he says, who falls on the pavement, so the fall of the wicked will come swiftly (Ecclus. 20). These are without doubt those who do not deserve to be shaken by the winnowing assaults of any misery, for whom an eternal sickness is nourished, nor to be beaten with the saints, the Lord chastising, with whom one reigns after the whips; of whom David makes mention in this song: They are not in the thoughts of men, and they shall not be scourged with men; therefore their pride has held them (Ps. 72). You see, then, that the undeserving are despised by the medicinal scourge, and the deserving are chastised in friendship. For God, the parent of all, as he is a faithful physician toward those he has taken in hand and a father toward his children whom he loves, so strikes in order to correct, not in order to kill. Therefore happy is he who is beaten, where the blow is one of love. Blessed is he whom the remedy of the heavenly lash cures, corrects, amends and sets in order; as David, the blessed and most illustrious prophet, sings in accord and cries out, saying: Happy is he whom you have amended, Lord, and whom you have taught out of your law (Ps. 93). Therefore, since by divine permission we lie subject to sicknesses of various sharpness, and lead a life that is to be cured by long calamity, let us bear with equanimity, for the testing of our virtue, the miseries foretold long ago. The unhappy and manifold misfortunes, anxieties and weeping into which we ran when we were born, let us carry with happiness of mind. Nor is it to be wondered at that the life of mortals is thus laid waste by the various slaughters of frequent evils in the world, in which no one is born laughing, in which no one begins the light of life except with tears. When at last the tent of the mother's womb showed us to the world, we came to know the world weeping, so that we might taste, as it were, the first-fruits of evils in our first tears. Solomon the prophet testifies with this declaration: I, he says, when I was born, received the common air, and fell upon the earth made alike [for all]; the first voice I uttered was like all others, weeping. I was nursed in swaddling clothes and with great cares. None of the kings had any other beginning of birth. There is therefore one entrance to life for all, and a like exit (Wisd. 7). For it is necessary that whoever has come should pass over from where he has led a pilgrim's life; especially since Solomon declares thus: There is one entrance, he says, to life, and a like exit. What prosperity or joy, then, can meet us where one first learns to weep, and where, among the very cradles of newborn infancy and in the very entrance of life, nothing else new from the world meets us but weeping? We trod the lights of the world with weeping; we shall indeed weep when we are about to pass over. O narrow and most anxious time of mortal life, where the end is named with the beginning, [and] we take up our beginning together with the end! He who is born is already captured by death. The dead are witnesses, since they do not deny that they were going to die. Therefore, since we have come as those who are to go, after the manner of pilgrims, let us conquer by bearing whatever befalls within the inn of the world, as passers-by: evils laid upon us are conquered when carried with good devotion. For an evil harms worse if it is borne badly; even good things hurt if they are borne badly. There indeed the solace of virtue is needed (namely in the contemplation of the heavenly reward), where the end and exit of life is longed for as the safety of the harbour is wished for at sea. For who, amid the anxieties of a wandering age and the distresses of harmful diseases, would not rather desire death than a long and languishing life, as Solomon says: Death is better than a bitter life, and eternal rest than lasting sickness (Ecclus. 30). And elsewhere: It is better for you to die than to live (ibid. 40). For death gives rest to every man. Certainly, amid raging evils, an exit is of necessity thirstily wished for. But just as it was not ours to be born, so neither is it in our power to die. Otherwise, if dying lay in our power, not dying would be in our power. We demand rest amid the straits of death for this reason, that amid evils it is a solace not to keep silent about the good: after the manner of sailors, for whom it is a refreshment amid hostile and anxious voyages to speak of the security of the harbour, at which, even if they may not arrive as quickly as the mind desires, it nevertheless helps, and is a fine thing, to wish for the better part. But since it is not in our power either to obtain the better things that are born from death, let us meanwhile, awaiting better things, wage a good contest amid evils. And a good contest is not to yield to evils, but to overcome evils by the good of virtue, through which we may be raised up into the better things that are born from death and are free from sickness and death. For without the leading and the bite of unhappiness we do not arrive at the triumphs of immortal glory, since the course into harbour is completed through dangers. Moreover, no one can be called a triumphant victor except one for whom virtue has found the victory, which sees everything that is feared crushed beneath it, and, unconquered, drags it captive.

CHAP. V. — For the world is like the sea, restless by nature and swelling even without winds, raising, that is, threatening and terrible waves even in calm itself; and though it may not harm its passengers, yet even a harmless greatness has something of dread, and fears and the blows of the waves are frequently not lacking to those who sail. Indeed, no helmsman has ever spread all his sails in security. So also in this world, we who pursue the crashing and turbulent course of this life are touched very frequently by the threats and occasions of evils: especially those whom the heavenly warfare has enclosed, sealed, within the royal camp. We have already said that the world is compared to the sea, in which prosperous things are rare and turbulent things are thick, there is dread and fear, diseases too are not lacking, and the only harbour of security is the exit. From this side and that the hostile onsets of calamity rush in; but up to the harbour, that is, up to the exit, it belongs to virtue to endure. Amid dangers the helmsman protects and keeps the ship. Amid calamities the mind, as ruler, steers and governs the man. Although someone may steer a manageable vessel when dangers have abated a little, yet rather that ship is awaited, and received with greater triumphs, which on a turbulent stream has mightily shaken off the blind waves rising into a whirl. Triumphal security receives it. Handsome is the soldier set in an army of arms; but the idle and empty man is squalid with a shapeless virtue, who on the field is neither known to himself nor known to another. For he lacks praises, and he lacks rewards too. And therefore danger ought not to be harmful where a reward is born. Nor ought a soldier to be called back or to suffer fear where the palm of victory follows. For he is wretched in his own happiness who has never deserved to have a conflict with the unhappinesses by which glory is begotten. Nor has he learned his own virtue whom calamity has not shaken. In short, with idle limbs the soldier lies ever ignorant of his own strength and unknown to himself, who has never panted in the glorious heats of hot wars, never found triumphs through sweat. Nor does the happiness of rewards follow him who will not carry the pack of arms. And therefore what generates reward ought to be in practice, and what brings forth glory ought to be desired. Therefore, since we must fight against the various darts of temptations: if anything arises that tests our strength, that shakes our limbs, that proves our soul, let us seize it with the embrace of virtue as an occasion of reward. Such ought to be the unconquered strength of the immovable virtue of the soul and of an unshaken mind, as is a rock in the sea which nature has founded amid the waves, which is beaten by the frequent collision of swelling waves and is not moved. So, where adversities call a man to battle, and calamity urges and drives him into the contest, let the happy mind lead him forth armed with the shield of virtue, and keep him safe and secure amid dangers, show him happy amid unhappy things, present him joyful amid anguish, sound amid sickly illnesses, and, calamity conquered, make him victor with the javelin of endurance. For disease is overcome in the body if the mind learns to endure: and therefore, where the body lies sick, a greater virtue must be nourished in the inner recesses, and [a strength] must be prepared which neither weariness may shake off nor age bend down.

CHAPTER VI. — Hold, then, brother, hold the unconquered strength of faith; hold the immovable Christian bulwark, founded on the firmness of heavenly vigour; amid languishing and very stiffened limbs, bear the shield of faith and of the soul unharmed and strong, and you will have conquered the sluggish disease and the ruinous languor. When evils batter like rams, meet them with the barriers of virtue. Conquer while you are beaten; for thus Christian power is nourished by hardships, and advanced by adverse evils. It befits the Christian warfare to be shaken by calamities and proved. It is its part to grow happily under unhappiness and distress, to grow up under afflictions, and, as it matures, to trample afflictions underfoot. It is its part to nourish its own bulwark by frequent exercises, and to have a contest with dangers. It is its part to sail to the harbour of everlasting happiness through the burning dangers of the world, and under the blows of medicinal discipline to reign powerfully over necessity itself. It is ours, I say, to be raised by the exercise of calamity to the summit of glory, and, while evils press upon us, to be advanced to good rewards. With us sickness, or any affliction whatever, is a proof of power, and certainly the mother of victorious virtue: just as the most blessed apostle Paul, amid various blows and diverse lashes and stormy assaults, set in the battle of diseases, as a heavenly armour-bearer powerful in infirmities, glories and says: Most gladly therefore will I glory rather in infirmities, that the power of Christ may dwell in me (2 Cor. 12): for which reason it pleases me to glory in infirmities, in insults, in necessities, in imperfections, in distresses for Christ's sake. For when I am weak, then I am strong (ibid.); and again: As often, he says, as I am weak, then I am more truly proved, and I am pleased with myself in my infirmities. And again, when he asked that the thorn of the flesh be taken from him, he learned that virtue can be nourished in infirmity: he says: There was given to me a thorn of my flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet me, so that I should not be exalted; for which reason I asked the Lord three times that it might depart from me; and he said to me: My grace is sufficient for you; for virtue is made perfect in infirmity (ibid.). Never, then, is virtue trained by softer lessons, since [otherwise] the examples of the greatest virtues would have perished. Our ship rejoices in tossings, when it is lifted up in whirlwinds, when it is beaten by raging waves, when this journey, made rugged by adversities rising up, does not spare [us], provoking devoted virtue into constant contest. For otherwise we cannot be happy with the Lord, unless it befalls us to be purged by unhappiness and by earthly squalor. Further, he must be judged wretched and sick who, enfeebled by pleasures, wallows and lies amid allurements. Let him know himself unhappy who wanders amid the delights of vices, pierced through by an enervated happiness. Wretched and unhappy is he who has not been tried by unhappiness. For he lacks the reward who lacks also the contest. He who dreaded the weapons of an adverse contest never deserved to obtain the name of victor. Without doubt it belongs to a prostrate mind to fear fearful things, to a lowly and sluggish one to pursue safe things. Virtue cast away into leisure without contest is an imperfect and feeble good. For vigour lies enervated and weak, the mind lies sick, brightness lies darkened; and therefore the bravest soldier must always stand in the battle line, and seek the occasion by which virtue, shaken out, may shine forth. For to a lover of battles wounds are ornaments. Therefore, for despising toils and for the knowledge of virtue, there is need of trials, the nourisher, that is, of strength to be built up. For that body is solid, and that mass of limbs robust, which frequent use has exercised. Farmers, indeed, have muscular strength from frequent work, and their hands are worn, while amid briars and thistles, with bent body, the crop is sought with sweat. The nautical art, whose ship the storm has often twisted while it makes for harbour amid dangers, has learned to pass through the waves and to fight with the tempest. A wounded army is strong for shaking off weapons, and seeks victories amid wounds, to please its own king. Runners' limbs are agile, and use, the master, has taught and trained them. Why say more? No one ascends to the more perfect parts without the onset of temptations, and seizes the reward as victor.

CHAPTER VII. — Therefore, while we first endure small and moderate things, it is necessary that we learn to bear greater or the greatest. For it is the bright mark of our warfare to set one's step through steep places, to be carried through hard things, and to bear the hard censure of miseries with hard strength. Our way to heaven lies through rough places, through narrow places, through hard windings and [rugged] places; and that way he has not held who was unwilling to be tried. To heaven God calls the bravest soldier, whom afflictions escort with glories accompanying, and rewards receive as a victor about to reign. Does he meanwhile lay on us anything sheer, which exceeds the measure of a balanced weight? Does he impose what by excess goes beyond the capacity of our virtue? The most faithful governor orders the burden to be laid on according to strength. This the proclamation of Paul attests and proves: God is faithful, he says, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear (1 Cor. 10). Let us believe that we are so driven and ruled by the Lord as pupils are ruled by teachers of schools: they impose and lay the most labour on those whom they see to excel the rest in clever talents; and we too adjust the burden for the animals subject to our dominion according to the measure of their strength: we lay strong loads on the stronger and small ones on the slender, so that use, that nourisher of virtue, may raise and advance their strength into the greatest robustness of youth. In this way our first lessons are beaten with light blows, so that thereafter they may prepare strength, made accustomed, for heavier ones, namely out of love of divine virtue. Although this reasoning abounds in many divine proofs, yet let us use some example also from worldly things; for it does no harm to use what belongs to others in that part in which it is ours. Do you suppose that their own children were hateful to the Spartans, whose natures and tender limbs, still ignorant of toil, they test, and, when public floggings are applied, paternal love itself exhorts them to bear the strokes of the whips bravely; and, when they are torn and half-dead, they entreat and beg them to persevere in setting wounds upon wounds? What wonder if God permits you and his noble children, his own household, to be hard tried for the brightness of nourishing virtue, intending to confer everlasting kingdoms on the victors? He thus promises the prizes of toil against all evils whatever, and says: Whoever perseveres to the end, he will be saved (Matt. 10). And again: Come to me, all who labour and are burdened, and I will give you rest (Matt. 11). A little of perishing time is the price of eternity. The devotion of tribulation will be repaid made fruitful with everlasting fruits. With us the kingdom is sought by a fruitful captivity; security is bought by dangers, rest is procured by sweat: For virtue, says the Apostle, is made perfect in infirmity (2 Cor. 12). It is certainly better to be shaken in the flesh by languid conditions than, with healthy limbs, to carry a conscience troubled by a blind punishment. For many fall sick with sins from the very idleness of the limbs. For while they are free from infirmities, the body must flow with a morbid slackness, and be dissolved by a deadly disease, and lead the man, wickedly healthy, headlong through vices and forests of errors...

CHAPTER VIII. — Do you judge those free, or strangers to diseases, whom barbarous pleasures have bound? They have no chain, but luxury holds them in bonds with a deadly bite. They have fallen into the snares of deadly pleasures like birds captured by the fowler's trick, which, the more they try to escape, the more they entangle themselves in countless knots and sink into deeper folds. Are those really healthy whom an insane disease wraps up and tosses about? Truly sound is he whom God corrects with any lash whatever, who by chastising shows himself a lover of man: Those whom I love, says the Lord, I rebuke and chastise (Rev. 3). And therefore let him not judge himself healthy who lacks either diseases or squalor, and is not strengthened by the remedy of infirmity. Those indeed are wretched who grow torpid in the sluggish tranquillity of excessive happiness; whom a counterfeit health flatters, to deceive and cheat them; whom, namely, an eternal sickness will hold, which will afterwards torment the whole man with an eternal torturer. Their ways are as many as the pleasures that come to their aid. Their road is the one which lust, their companion, itself destined to perish, dictates through dangers. For seized by the windings of dragging vices, the wretched are rolled with various falls into destruction, on a most uncertain way, never to return; they stretch the mind toward outward things, after the manner of streams, which never flow back to their own source. Indeed they lead this life, whose companion is its end, with prosperous courses, as they themselves suppose; but the step at the last ends altogether badly, while at the very end one stands hard. And what does it profit to have run prosperously through dangers, if after the course it befalls one to perish? In vain, indeed, does a ship run into harbour through a proud and raging sea, with friendly waves and favourable prosperity, if it arrives with shipwreck, and the harbour receives it to perish. It is better, therefore, to arrive at the harbour of glory under the leading of any affliction whatever, than, after completing the course of morbid slackness in a delicate ship, to go out into punishments. Often, then, poverty is better than riches, deformity than beauty, insult than praises, servitude than power, weakness than strength, captivity than liberty, lowliness than rank. David, the illustrious prophet, expressed a song of this kind: It is good for me, Lord, he says, that you have humbled me, that I may learn your justifications (Ps. 118). Therefore it is better to be humbled by the losses of discipline by [God's] judgement than to be condemned with the world, as the Apostle says: When we are judged by the Lord, we are corrected, so that we may not be condemned with this world (1 Cor. 11). Therefore what is bestowed for our benefit out of the Lord's love, let us bear without murmuring. For discipline is applied by the Lord as a remedy by a physician. It belongs to the art of medicine sometimes to work with fire and iron. What wonder if the Lord, the physician of our souls, shakes us with whirlwinds, tests us with diseases, purges us with calamities? It belongs to our fortitude to be purged as if through fires and flames, in the manner of vessels, which divine Scripture attests and proves: The furnace, it says, proves the potter's vessels, and the trial of tribulation just men (Ecclus. 27). And elsewhere it says: Gold, and silver, and iron, and lead, and everything that has passed through fire, will be cleansed (Num. 31). Vessels never say to the potter: Why do you test us by the judgement of the flames, and burn and prove us with cooking fires? Unless the fire as judge pronounces them most fit by its judgement, they cannot be in use. We too, unless the judgement or testing of temptations has purged us, are found useless to the potter of our members, who burns us to cure us, tries us to free us, harasses us to save us. For nothing is so defiled, so filthy, that it is not cleansed of vices by purgings. Often, indeed, we have seen those soiled by reproach come into brightness, and iron covered with rust shine again with its former face. We have seen gold and silver purged by the discipline of the flame, and pruned trees revive with most joyful cultivation and be adorned with lovely shoots. We have seen barren things recalled to fruitfulness, and, the trunk being exhausted, the root accompanied by a very great crop. So too in us, whatever perhaps was seething under the pressure of sins, whatever stain of squalid old age stood in the way, has been shut out by the light of sickness. And therefore, brother, the sickness of your limbs, acting as a physician, has rendered you healthy. In you only the matter of the flesh lacks the health of strength; and lest it perhaps should trouble you, it is troubled by a useful disease. This is what the dog-star of old age strikes in all men, and, like hay, it withers, about to lose its own flower, as it is written: All flesh is hay, and all its glory like the flower of hay. The hay has withered, and the flower has fallen; but the word of the Lord remains for ever (Isa. 40). Let us therefore bear with equanimity if the body, which we read will perish like hay with its flowers falling, is tossed about exhausted by harmful evils, the body whose health has been wont to bring disease upon the soul, and to draw out deadly and barbarous pleasures against spiritual benefits. Often, indeed, the unbridled flesh has ungirded the soldiers of chastity. It is for our good, then, if we are chastised with long and biting scourges, [the flesh] by which nevertheless our chastity is assailed. Foolishly we love the flesh: we do not grieve over the prison and tomb of the soul. Therefore, scorning the fragility of the flesh itself, let us seize as a treasure, with the embraces of devotion, whatever befalls. It is timid for a Christian soldier to wish to remain in calm, after the manner of those who make merry. It belongs to a downcast mind to dread the whirlwind, but to an opposing one not to tremble amid opposing things. It belongs to unhappiness not to know adversity, to happiness to know how to engage with adversities, and to know how to fight. For since all the blows by which we are shaken, as we have already said, are born from a divine gift, let him know himself a stranger to the love of God who does not know how to be harassed by temptations, since the trumpet of the law impresses on our hearing with manifold song and says: The Lord your God tests you, it says, to know whether you love him with all your heart and with all your soul (Deut. 13). And elsewhere: Son, it says, do not neglect his discipline, and do not faint when you are corrected by him. For whom God loves he corrects (Prov. 3). And again: Do not despise the correction of the Lord, it says. For he himself gives pain, and he himself refreshments; he strikes, and his hands bestow health (Job 5).

CHAPTER IX. — But perhaps you say: THE SICK MAN. If only, as with others, it were granted to be tried at intervals, in the hope of health! If only I might taste health a little in the gap of some success or other! What is this, that disease so dwells in my limbs and lives shut up [there] that it has shut out health, never to return? That as a deadly companion it leads my shaken limbs to the very end of life, and is itself led off too, to be shut out by death together with the limbs? What is this, that my limbs have been cheated of the sense of health through the whole span of life? Once the cold has entered my veins, their warm vigour has vanished into chill; the numbness shut within has shut out the steps that nature had given. In short, not even a little walking is tasted for the exercise of my wasting body. My knees are not bent in the accustomed prayers; the uneven row of my fingers, disordered by an inner numbness, is kept from handling things as it used to. Why say more? Every function of the body that once used to attend on the positions of the sinews is thus frozen, shut in. Oh grief! I alone was meant to be chastised like this: I alone to lie beneath such deadly blows, and to be wrapped in long-lasting evils. JEROME. I beg you, brother, keep back these murmurs with the reins of patience, and shut in your complaining words with silence, while the prophetic consolation addresses you thus and says: Join yourself to God, it says, and endure, that your life may grow at the last. Accept everything that is laid upon you, and endure in pain, and in your humiliation have patience, since gold and silver are tested in fire, but acceptable men in the furnace of humiliation (Ecclus. 2). When I review the decrees of the law and the songs of the prophets, my hearing also takes in excellent sayings of worldly authority, stolen, unless I am mistaken, from the divine law, which may properly be set among the precepts of the law. For it does no harm to use what belongs to others in that part where it is ours. This is the first saying: Fire, it says, tests gold, and misery good men. And elsewhere: Nothing, it says, seems more unhappy than the man to whom nothing adverse has ever happened. He has not been able to test himself, since everything has flowed for him according to his wish. And elsewhere: I judge you wretched, it says, because you have not been wretched; you have passed through life without an adversary: no one will know what you could have done, not even you yourself. For there is need of trial for knowledge of oneself. What each man can do he has not learned unless he has been tried. And elsewhere: For to be happy for a long time, and to pass through life without a sickness of the mind, is to be ignorant of the other part of the nature of things. Therefore let us bear with a happy mind the miseries that arise, by which unknown things are learned and happiness is born, and vice too, shaken out, is purged: whether because we ought to suffer, or because we are already held captive. Unless the flame has added brightness to gold, it suffers worthlessness, darkened by impurities; so he who has not been shaken out by the trials of miseries lies ignorant of the parts of happiness and of his own virtue. Rightly Solomon testifies with this saying: He who has not been tried in anything does not know what sort of man he is (Ecclus. 34). Bless the Lord, therefore, in the time of tribulation, whom you praised in the time of health. Use the songs of the prophetic voice: I will bless the Lord, it says, at all times, his praise always in my mouth (Ps. 33). Let that saying of blessed Job above all be brought forth from you with steadfast proclamation, by which failing strength rejoices in great nourishment, and rises up restored in a new shoot: If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not endure evil things (Job 2)? The Lord gave, the Lord has taken back: as it seemed good to the Lord, so it has been done: blessed be the name of the Lord (Job 1). It is therefore hostile and quite contrary, in the time of testing, to murmur against the Lord: who either harasses the pestilent stain of our life with the tossing of hardships in order to free [us], or winnows [us] for righteousness in order to crown [us], and by the harassing of the limbs either a fault is beaten, or righteousness is tested so that it may conquer. For so that we may turn your mind back to the palms of ancient testing for the consolation of your sufferings, let us use the examples of the most righteous.

CHAPTER X. — Although it is known that the merits of persons differ by long steps, it is not unfair if we compare the struggle of a Christian man with the combats of victorious righteousness. What you see yourself bearing in this world is moderate, if you review what Job, the Lord's intimate, was able to endure with the Lord's permission. God has tempered [it] so that it would fit and match your strength. Could you, who are unequal, have borne the first [trials], when the titles of righteousness are not equal? You are struck less than the righteous man, but you are wounded more heavily than the rest: his [sufferings] are great, but yours are not lesser. For you are yourself great, who follow a great man. This Job was one, a patriarch, an unconquered worshipper of the Majesty, wealthy and rich in the riches of equity, whose illustrious merits the Lord stood witness to, when he forestalled the deadly instruments of the hostile faction with a proclamation of praise: Have you noticed my servant Job, that there is no one like him on earth: a man without complaint, a true worshipper of God, keeping himself from every evil work, and remaining in his innocence and in simplicity of heart (Job 1)? So when by divine permission he was struck by hostile darts, and the frequent savage insinuation of the robber assailed him, he defeated the blows that arose with the shield of patience, and, strong with the barriers of righteousness, he met the deadly forest of oncoming evils, full of arrows and crosses. He, when his wealth was taken away by the hostile whirlwind, felt no loss, for he found gain in losses, for he possessed the Lord shut within the folds of his breast. He, when a sudden force twisted the building into collapse with its corners shaken, was bereaved of his children taken away, and remained steadfast and immovable in faith. When his innocent limbs, full of the Lord, bred worms with legions of beasts, and a deadly mass of worms wandered through the tunnels of the dug-up flesh of the body wounded with hostile blows, lying amid wounds he fought on unharmed. And he whom a hostile rage was devouring with pestilent sores bore the enemy's whirlwinds with tranquillity of mind, so that they gave way. The righteous man conquered by being beaten; the enemy failed by striking. To him the service of his own attendants was denied; around you your own perform the services of servants. Your friends console you with frequent visits and grieve, so that, if nature permitted, they would perhaps carry this burden with you. There is one, brother, one virtue of the mind which, plucking us out of the whirlwinds of this life as from the sea, leads us into the harbour of tranquillity. See, the day hastens with steep descent to its setting. Behold, the unclean world, with the filth of old age, rolls towards its fall. Behold, by the vote of death heaven receives the victors. All things perish as we escape, and, with their setting now near, are swallowed up never to return. With us, after the world is lost, after the death of the body, all things are healed. We shall rejoice in the soundness of our limbs, where life will be troubled by no disease. Therefore in you, brother, let a most excellent mind so govern and direct the hindered functions of the body with illustrious leadership, that this calamity of the body may be a longed-for occasion of virtue. For no tree is solid or robust except one that is tested by the onset of constant whirlwind, its trunk shaken and bent this way and that, or into which the blast of the whirling winds often rushes; for by these very harassments it is bound tight, pressed, and with its roots fixed is more surely strengthened. So we, stretched out, are fortified by the biting scourges of frequent evils, corrected by being beaten, bound tight by being struck, and we are free of filth while we are winnowed by long misfortunes. Therefore amid increasing pains, and with the limbs afflicted by monstrous miseries, let virtue reign, robust and unharmed with heavenly vigour, by which contrary things may be borne, and those benefits that are called adversities. Amid these very straits the wise man, with an equal support of consolation, rejoices and wastes away, and by ambitious reason is enlarged and lives. In short, he ignores what he suffers who is mindful of unconquered virtue, who under the guidance of reason has found that many were oppressed by evils, and by their own evil, with reason as teacher, were increased and nourished. Therefore the consolations of reason lie open to you, so that the calamity of the body may now be held as a benefit, and the fact that the mass of the whole body lies captive. But the resurrection will come, to restore you unharmed, and all the limbs that in you are seized. But let your tongue be nourished with daily matter for the praises of the Lord, as it will tell an abundance of praise in the heavenly kingdoms. May the Lord cherish you with heavenly medicine, and grant you to endure under such a weight with unbending virtue.
LETTER II.
To a sick friend, on the perfect man.

SECOND NOTICE

That this letter too is unworthy of Marianus has been shown by us in the preface to the appendix. Now the variant readings of this letter, which we have appended, were excerpted from codex 9, Plut. XIX, of the Laurentian Library in Florence, page 337.

CHAP. I. — See, I am writing to you again, and I find nothing worthy that it would befit your wisdom to read. And is it any wonder if, with you absent, as though deserted by the sun, the wit of a cold heart freezes, and the mind, a stranger to the light, grows numb, smothered by the cloud of folly, and I am the less wise the more widely I am separated from you? But if at present anything in my discourse pleases you, it will be granted to me by your prayers. Then, so that you may recognise all my folly more thoroughly, I also treated my stomach, after I had taken that wax plaster, while you were absent, from which I deserve to suffer worse: for, after your holy ministry and angelic service, I laid the hands of physicians on it, as though there were no prophet in Israel, when, if I was suffering anything, it ought to have been easier for me to return to you than to think like a pagan; and better to endure the toil of even the hardest journey than to be cheated of so precious a sight as the sight of you, so that any compensation whatever should rather follow than that I should come to the fly-religion of Ekron. These things this world suggested to me in your absence, which in your presence would have no counsel in me. For you had made me a council-house of prophets, not a little gathering of sirens. But now the whole senate of folly, entering into me to destroy your holy work against me, deals with me in fourfold form. For it exacts interest from the absent, which it did not presume to do with you present, so that you may understand that if I was wise in anything with you, according to God, what I was wise in was yours. So, while Moses was absent, the people of Israel committed fornication (Exod. 32); so in the boat, while the Lord slept, the apostles were troubled by the storm (Matt. 8). So in the porticoes of Bethsaida [the water] does not know the man who has not the water of the saving pool (John 5). How great another kind of fault I notice here too! I cared for the little body while the soul languished; I cherished the outer man while the inner was sick: I came to the aid of human things while divine things were in distress, bent by the vice of common custom, by which we are all careful in the smallest matters and negligent in the greatest. And this happens because we do not know where true life is. That is, this sun misleads us, this day deceives us, this expanse gets round us. The world leads us on, while we think that there is nothing more than itself, and we suppose that light is what we see with our eyes; and we judge that the man is what we perceive, and we believe that the world goes along with life, not knowing where the man is, and what the man is, and what the life of that man is: if we understood this, we would not be born for one thing and live for another. So, having deserted the origin of life, we have lost also the reason for living. And first let us hear where this man is of whom we are speaking.

CHAP. II. — Since the division itself has given rise to a certain discussion for us, understand that he is contained within this body, which was formed from the mud of the earth by the hand of God the craftsman, as in a kind of little vessel, as the Apostle says: We have this treasure in earthen vessels (2 Cor. 4); he, poured throughout this body, has shared with the flesh a vital sense, which does not fail itself. He rules, he is not ruled; and he possesses rather than is possessed, so that he does not receive life but supplies it. For when the clear spirit animated this earthly and sluggish matter, taken up for the use of service, he becomes lord of the body, not a man under the body. Then this little vessel I spoke of lives while he is present, and dies when he departs. This one, then, visible and perishable, is the dwelling, or the servant, or the sheath of that inner one. But he himself, who is truly the man, since he is the second, is the place of the division made; as he is invisible, so all his things must be invisible. The hands of physicians cannot reach him if he is sick; he is not restored by the juices of herbs if he fails. Nothing bodily can enter him; only the likeness of his own substance comes down to him; he is healed by the word, he recovers by obedience. Then, when in the Church of Laodicea he seemed to himself, according to the outer man, both blessed and rich, and keen-sighted, and well clothed, he is rebuked by the Lord, and it is said to him: Do you not know that you are wretched, and pitiable, and poor, and blind, and naked (Rev. 3)? He, surely, as I said, was held to be neither without clothing, nor without eyes, nor without riches. But that invisible God of ours saw that invisible man to be in poverty, in blindness, in nakedness; and he even deigns to urge him to buy from him gold refined by fire, and white clothing, in which he may be most gloriously clothed, and eye-salve, by which he may recover his sight. He has, then, his own eyes besides these fleshly ones, which he can either lose or heal; and he is, by his own standard, naked, so much so that he needs clothing: but in a wonderful way the Lord speaks [as] to a physician, as he himself says, and bids him buy riches from him. With what goods, if he is both naked and poor, will he buy either that most noble garment or that gold already purged by fire? From where can the outlay for such a trade come? Clearly, if he either transfers the profits of the outer man, or grows rich by not using the very things by which he seemed rich outwardly; and if he blinds the eyes of the body, by which he was carried off by burning desire for worldly things, through contempt of the corrupt universe. So that invisible man, who, as we have said, is truly the man, is both raised up in contempt of this outer one, and clothed by nakedness, and enlightened by blindness. So Jacob, through bodily blindness, discerned not only the places but also the merits of his grandsons Ephraim and Manasseh (Gen. 48). For when Joseph his son, who was presenting the aforesaid little ones, judged that he did not see [even what was] before his feet, he perceived in his father's reply that he foresaw even what was to come. But as that inner man makes this outer one live by his life, and animates him by watering him from the fountain of his own nature: so in turn the outer, through the corruption of his deadly matter, kills the inner, if he has bound him with unlawful desires. And though the one seems to be of a different nature from the other, each passes into the substance of the victor, so that either the spiritual, by his virtues, makes even the carnal spiritual, or the flesh, as victor, makes the soul carnal. Then, when the Lord in anger was thinking of destroying the human race, he said: My Spirit shall not remain in men, because they are flesh (Gen. 6). And since we are surely all clothed with flesh, and yet without doubt are not in the flesh, we who do not walk according to the flesh, from this also it results that a man is not always reckoned by this name of 'man'. For according to his virtues or vices he takes on both forms and names. Thus the prophet says: Do not become like the horse and the mule (Ps. 31). There are, then, men who before the Lord are horses and mules. And the Lord says: Do not throw your pearls before swine (Matt. 7). There are, then, men who are also swine. And again the Lord himself: See, I send you as sheep in the midst of wolves (Matt. 10). There are, then, men who are also wolves; and on the contrary there are men who are also sheep. And the Lord says further to Peter: Feed my sheep (John 21); and he himself earlier: Come after me, and I will make you a fisher of men (Matt. 4). There are, then, men who are also fish. But these seem to be forms of actions, not of bodies. For the state of our body is fixed, as of all living creatures; but since before God we are judged not by the state of our body but by the merits of our life, it appears that every man forms for himself by his own mind his state and name. This surely comes about through either the fault or the virtue of that invisible man whom we are describing. For it is his vice if, [being meant to rule], he has allowed himself to be subjected; if, against the divine ordering, there is servitude in lordship and lordship in servitude. But lest I seem (since, the wall, as it were, having been thrown down a little, I have come in my discussion to that invisible man) to destroy the body altogether, which is of so great a mystery that in this very [body], that is, in our frail and weak one, the Lord came, I have not done this, nor am I doing it; but I have tried to show that the life of this outer man consists in the life of that inner one; and again that the death of the inner comes down from the death of this one: where poison has been administered through vices, this one has nothing of life; unless watered by that one, he holds nothing; and the one passes into the nature of the other, as I said, either infected by vices or cleansed by virtue. Therefore, since I have now shown, if only briefly, both where the man is and what the man is, let us now see what the life of that man is. For if this worldly life, which takes evils for goods and goods for evils, which the whole world follows and cultivates, is not in abundance of riches, nor in the height of power, nor in the cunning of jurisdiction, nor in the pomp of eloquence, nor in strength made glorious by battles, nor in goods growing by exchange of provinces and by one's own travelling abroad, nor in the allure of beauty, nor in the canvassing of gifts, nor finally in all these things which we see, since all these things perish, and without them people commonly live happily even by the world's standard: that, then, is true life, a life to be revered: to know God, to fear his power, to love his love, to marvel at the world in its maker, to despise the interloper, to be content with modest food according to the need of nature, protected by cheap clothing either for the sake of modesty or against the harshness of the season. So, too, to touch the rest of creation not according to its abundance, nor for the sake of [luxurious] living, but for the support of this light. For whatever is more than this is from evil: to love every man as a brother, to harm no one, to serve all, to bear the form of a servant with the Lord, who, besides the ministry that is held within, serves us daily in the world, bringing forth the sun, sending out light, pouring down rains, varying the seasons, both producing and ripening the crops. For he serves us in the face and in the abundance of all creation, since he brought forth all things for us. But to return to the duties of man: to cover the naked, to feed the hungry, to give drink to the thirsty, to visit the sick, to grieve with the sorrowful, to bury the dead, to keep nothing for oneself as one's own, but to judge all one's things common with all, and then to live more for oneself when one is thought to live for others, and to store up for oneself when one is believed to be giving out to others. And yet these still touch on the features of the outer man.

CHAP. III. — But that life of the inner man consists in the knowledge of divine things. It does not consist in knowing in what part of the earth the sky revolves, or whether the stars are swept along in a contrary course, or whether the fullness of the sea produces its increase from Ocean, or whether its very roundness holds the globe of the world suspended, or whether a four-sided form binds it with jutting corners, or whether the world itself is one or there are several. For these things do not serve the benefit of the soul, and before God they are judged foolish. Rather, the soul lives and is fed when it is occupied with sound thoughts. And what are these sound thoughts? Without doubt they are these: when our mind remembers its own author; when, as if through a kind of coming to its senses, it venerates and contemplates him as its maker; when it marvels at his works, in order to see him in his works. As blessed Paul says: For his invisible things are seen from the creation of the world, being understood through the things that have been made, and also his eternal power and divinity (Rom. 1). That is, they are sound when we stretch out from the immense visible things of creation to the whole of the invisible Creator, and, while we learn through these things that he is beyond estimation, we [yet] form an estimate of him. They are sound when, unfolding his height through the gift of the Holy Spirit (since he alone admits us into him who is from him), we look upon all the beginnings of rising creation as though we had been made by him before them; and when we gaze upon the things God made as though he were making them still. Running through the whole origin of the world, we become, as it were, older than we are in age; and although all things were made before we existed, yet, while we are grafted onto their author, we regard the nature of all things as though it had been brought forth through us. We entered into it not to serve but to rule. So let us be separated from worldly wisdom, which ascribes all things either to chance or to atoms, and be raised up by divine meditations. Through his help let us be separated from those who said that matter always existed, and wanted God to be merely the craftsman of things; or from those who worshipped these very elements as gods; or from those who brought in families of gods by sexes, by ages, by functions, as if a common people subject to the senses. Let us be set apart by the Holy Spirit, and drawn up to higher things, living the true life, that is, being wise with the true wisdom which this folly lacks. Let us remember that the world was made by God out of nothing, and that all living creatures, which did not exist by nature, came when they were called by God, the Word being the maker. For to him alone is it lawful to call the things that are not as though they were. Let us remember that this very man, for whom so great a possession was being prepared, was made after his own image not by some Prometheus out of a myth, but by that founder of the universe, who deigned to make him from the slime of the earth with his own hand as well, so that no part of him might be absent in us. This thought, as I said, is the life of the soul; for this is the first principle of living, that the soul should not be ignorant of the one to whom it owes itself; that it should not be deceived into venerating another besides him; that it should not adore the servants of its life as though they were the authors of life; that it should not marvel at the elements so much as to judge them unworthy to be believed made, when he is rather to be admired who produced things so admirable. O how majestic is this divine thought, and how full of life! O how greatly it kindles man himself to every pursuit of goodness! O how greatly it commends to him the majesty of his author, when he considers that in all creation nothing besides himself was formed by the hand of God: not the earth, not the seas, not the sky, nor finally the stars, so bright, so pure, so shining. Man alone, from a kind of slime, of a heavier and dirtier element, was formed by that right hand whose palm measures the sky in measure, whose fist encloses the spaces of the earth that lies so boundless. So great a thing it was that he once came to be. Let us see, however, how much the kindness of the Creator favours him besides, in not making him from the stars. For if he had been created from there, he would have been strong rather through the brightness of his material than through the condescension of his maker, since he himself would appear lesser than the origin of his body. If, made from heavenly things, he were brought down to earth to till the land, [it would be less glorious for him than] to be soon raised from the soil and set above the stars. Our God, I say, wanted what we are to be his own, properly his own, so that we would owe nothing to matter, nothing to the elements, nothing to any first principles, whether great or very small. If the mind, turned in on itself, goes over and considers all these things, they become more modest and narrower than our own beginnings. But when, through the touch of the hand of God that formed us, we ceased to be what we had been, and our nature, lying open to a new quality of matter, was glorified for its maker through the transformation of the element, and among the elements there began to be, if it may be said, a new element of our body, at once we were made more exalted than all the bodies of the world, not by the substance of our nature but by the power of the Founder, through whom there arose from what lies beneath the other creatures that which would command all creatures. Indeed, if you look at the material of our flesh and body, you will find nothing lower, nothing cheaper, nothing more subject to every injury and suffering. Earth alone seems to be the handmaid of the other elements; it alone feels in itself the powers of all, not without loss to itself, whether when it is scattered as dust by the winds, or when, soaked, it is swallowed up by the waves, or when, baked by the fires of the stars, it is consumed: so that man not only cannot boast that he is from it, but may even blush for it. But if we contemplate our standing, which is more excellent than the other living beings, since God brought him in formed after his own image, you will find that the earth itself is the seed of our body. If there were any sense in it, it could have rejoiced that because of us, in whom it received the image and likeness of the Creator, it was made happier by being changed than it was when it arose. For the hand of God touched it, a touch which it did not itself merit, since it was done for another's sake. For what is more splendid than this standing? What higher thing shall we be able to know? What is so carefully arranged into limbs? What so gracefully bent at the joints? What so loftily raised up in face and eyes? What so tunefully modulated into words? What so vividly animated in heart? What richer in sense? What more hidden in thought? What more abundant in speech? What stronger in intellect? What better equipped in ordering? What more retentive in memory? What more gentle in affection? What more exalted in reflection? So that it plainly appears that he adorned that first-formed man even then with every dignity, or rather adorned in this body the standing of his Son, our God, who was to come at the end of the ages for our redemption. To him also at that time [God] gave paradise, like a most delightful estate, both graced with refinements of the town and planted with country produce, given under the law of death; and that first sower [of evil] begrudged it, and, deceiving the credulous newness of the first humans, secretly sank his poison into our bodies, and cut apart, by a kind of discord of division, the single and perfect nature of man made from two substances: so that, whereas we had one mind, that is, the one which the kinship of soul and body produced, he brought forth through the corrupted nature another will against the soul. And so the Apostle says: I see another law in my members fighting against the law of my mind, and taking me captive in the law of sin which is in my members (Rom. 7). And elsewhere: The flesh lusts against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh. These are opposed to each other, so that you do not do whatever you wish (Gal. 5).

CHAP. IV. — Hence also this Founder of ours, who had made either us for ourselves or the world for us, was offended by those first humans and poured out curses on each, as the size of the crime required. And although angry, yet he soon showed, like a loving father, the mystery of our salvation. Nor would it have been right to think of the remedy for our salvation at any other time than the one at which death had been discovered. So the wiser apply a physician to death at the very first, so that once the source of the illness is detected, a saving remedy may come to the aid more easily.
