Therefore our Lord and Saviour was not promised only when Isaiah cries: Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son (Isa. 7), and when it was said to Abraham: At this time I will come, and Sarah will have a son (Gen. 18). For this was already almost too late, and so many thousands of patriarchs would seem to have died without hope; and they surely could not have had life if they had not hoped that the Lord would come, as the Apostle says: For we are saved by hope. For hope that is seen is not hope, but that which is hoped for (Rom. 8). And what sort of hope could there have been, if it had not been promised? Rather, just as that beast, wiser than all the beasts, had the wisdom to bring death upon the first man, so it was fitting that the Lord, the true Wisdom, should already at that time have the wisdom of a life-giving help; and this he did. Nor did he cease to proclaim it, lest so great a work of his, driven back by one battering-ram of the enemy, should seem to have been brought forth without any protection, for a fall rather than for glory; and at the same time lest he should be held stronger who had been able to overthrow so great a work of another's power, than he would be if he either could not have preserved his work, which he made ineffably above all creatures, or had been unwilling to restore it. He defended himself, I say, from this reproach. That Founder and Redeemer of ours defended himself, and showed that he was equally able and willing; for neither did the strength of power fail him, nor condescension fail his love. This is the more to be adored by us, that in the very storm of our error it did not stand still, but even burst forth greater while it was provoked: since where we deserved punishment, the hope of redemption is shown, and in the bitter danger of shipwreck the harbour of salvation is opened, so that in a new way what had been the matter of wrath began to be the origin of mercy. Thus he made plain by a secret working that he wished our weakness to be a proof of his power, and showed how greatly he loved us even while we sinned against him, since he could not forget us even after our errors; rather, he redeemed us at a higher price than he had made us. Let human cruelty now seek out for criminals either private workhouses or public prisons, let it sigh with anger amid iron manacles and fetters stiff with a hard beam, and let it loosen its ingenuity on manifold inventions of punishment; and let every judge, with head held high, prove the purity of his own mind by another's peril, the more a friend to atrocity the more he is a stranger to crime. For those who are purer of guilt are usually the more savage towards the guilty. They pursue the misdeeds or the contagion of criminals the more zealously, the less and the more carelessly they themselves have avoided fellowship in crimes. O wretches, endowed with every blindness, who adorn good with evil, who exalt self-restraint under a show of cruelty, and commend their own cruelty by others' misfortune, when they lend their virtues in support of the ruin of the wretched, and the innocence of the one judging applauds the torments of the guilty.

CHAP. V. — But our God, against all hope, against almost all belief, finding good in evil out of the riches of his mercy, begetting and strengthening love in the midst of anger, willed that the seed of sinning should turn out into the fruit of showing mercy; and he who ought to have destroyed us for our transgression promised that he would restore us for the sake of his mercy. And at that very time when we deserved punishments, he showed a proof of salvation, so that we could understand how much he would be able to bestow when not offended, who gave so much when angered. So in the first man, while he was speaking, he at once pledged us help in the very judgment, at once brought forth good things from his good treasure, at once made public the mystery, unknown even to the angels, which was to be fulfilled in the last time, and promised to the earthly Adam an Adam from heaven. For when he struck the serpent with a curse, as it deserved, he ordered it to have earth for food and to creep on its belly; and since it had itself brought about that death, he added, saying: And I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and the seed of the woman. She shall tread on your head, and you shall watch for her heel (Gen. 3). Do you not consider, do you not see, what he was then threatening it with in Christ? For I understand no other seed of the woman at all except that of which the Apostle says: Made of a woman, made of flesh (Gal. 4); that of which, as the evangelist (Luke 3) says, he was thought to be the son of Joseph, but was not; that, surely, by which the Word was made flesh (John 1). For if we look at the common and natural process of generation, women do not have seed; indeed no woman conceives without a man; and therefore, since already then in Adam the seed of human generation had been corrupted by transgression, a heavenly seed is promised, not, as the Apostle understands it, from the corruption of a man, but from God: so that when it became flesh in the woman, it would also naturally fit to itself the elements of bodily substance, that is, of moisture and blood, in the very vessel in which those elements are placed. And so the Mother of our Lord Jesus Christ was promised already then in that woman. She is set against the enmity of the serpent: I will put, he says, enmity between you and the woman (Gen. 3); he certainly does not say 'I put', lest this should seem to refer to Eve. It is a word of promise, which is carried over into the future. I will put, he says, enmity between you and the woman: that woman, surely, who would bring forth the Saviour, not the one who would bear a fratricide. I will put, he says, enmity between you and the woman, who, having rejected readiness to believe, not only would not listen to you, were you to point to the sweetness of fruit as the opening of the eyes, or promise that she would be like gods; but even when Gabriel himself brought the word, she would demand an account of the newness of the promise, saying: How shall this be, since I have not known a man (Luke 1)? That woman, surely, whom golden modesty made tremble at the sight of the angel, yet whom ardour of faith and a steadfastness that knew no slipping made bold to inquire the reason; and she who gave to him at his coming, out of modesty, her silence, did not, out of wonder, yield to him as he promised. For in her concern she inquired about what was being announced. And so the angel did not rebuke unbelief, as in Zechariah, but instructed her about the newness of the divine working, saying: The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you (Luke 1). Behold that seed of the woman, which would not be poured into the womb by a transmission through the mingling of both sexes in the work of generation, but would be found in the womb of an unviolated virgin with the enclosure shut. And so the prophet, while promising a new thing full of wonder, carries it out with a new word: Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb, and shall bear a son (Isa. 7). Daily, surely, we both see and hear of the necessity of procreation; yet of no woman is it said 'she conceived in the womb', since the substance of the future human being, poured in through the man, grows together in the woman, and the woman's womb is not the beginning of the human being to be born but the nourishment of what has been deposited. But Mary was not so much the first as the only one to conceive in the womb, she whose untouched modesty produced the conception of the womb without loss of virginity: who alone bore for us what she did not receive from us, as the Lord says: You are from below, I am from above (John 8). She alone is mother to a son while being a virgin to her husband; whose conception the birth made known while her virginity was unaware of it; who alone was called woman not by conceiving but by giving birth. From her, therefore, is the promised seed of the woman, who according to the manhood is our Lord God, who was not poured into the womb but found [there], as the evangelist confirms when he says of Mary: She was found having in the womb (Matt. 1). See, what had been announced does not depart from the prophet's preceding saying: A virgin shall conceive in the womb; but in the newness of the mystery it agrees even in likeness of wording, and the account of the deed is described in the same style in which [the prophet] announces that it is to be done. The prophet Isaiah says: A virgin shall conceive in the womb; Matthew reports: She was found having in the womb (ibid.). The outcome answers to the very word of the promise, since the evangelist speaks no differently from the seer, nor is he thrown into confusion by the difficulty of finding an expression to convey the newness of the deed. Where are the grammarians? Where are the counsellors? What school produced these men, so that they should speak beyond custom? What school showed them the newness of a teaching so plainly marked? They do not speak by human sense, since what they speak of is not a human work. And yet they so mark a new thing never done before, that you understand that with a wonderful deed a wonderful mode of speech was also born. Let us go back, then, to the holy women of the patriarchs, and see whether it is so written of any of them. We read of Sarah: And the Lord visited Sarah, as he had said. And God did for Sarah as he had spoken to her, and she conceived and bore Abraham a son (Gen. 21). In Isaac the divine kindness is shown in these words: And God heard him, and Rebecca his wife conceived (Gen. 25). And so of Jacob's wives it is put thus: And Leah conceived and bore Jacob a son (Gen. 29), etc. Of none of these, surely, is it written 'she conceived in the womb', though whatever they conceived they could not conceive outside the womb; but since they knew they had conceived from union with a man, conception did not come to them with virginity preserved; Mary alone conceived in the womb, since with the seminal entrance unopened she conceived with the womb shut. Toward the seed of this conception, if we reason rightly and handle divine things more inwardly, there went before, as a figure for its time, that decree which bound the firstborn with blessings or obligations, as the Lord says: Every male that opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord (Exod. 13). What is this male that opens the womb, when it is not the necessity of childbirth that opens the wombs of all women, but knowledge by a husband? And so no woman is called a virgin after a husband, so that the word 'shut' seems suited to the mysteries to come. And above we showed that Scripture has of Rachel: And God heard her, and opened her womb, and she conceived. Certainly it did not say first 'she conceived' and afterwards 'he opened her womb'; but first 'he opened': that is, so that the husband, the doors of the womb being opened, might enter as one about to sow a ploughed field with seeds. Then it adds: and she conceived. So it was not by birth but by conception, or rather, for conception, that it was opened; and it designated not the one to be brought forth, at his birth, but the one who was to sow the one to be brought forth. And if she was opened already before conception, in order indeed that she might conceive, surely the one who was born could not open her, being only spoken of as about to be born, who could not even be conceived while she was shut: Every male, he says, that opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord (Luke 2). What is this principle, which does not seem fulfilled even according to the sense? Jacob fraudulently seizes the place of the first brother, and is neither barred by the order of birth nor condemned for his deceit. The sons of Joseph are marked by their grandfather with a blessing reversed against the order of birth; nor was the blindness of one who foresaw the future [a hindrance], nor did the son, warning him, bend aside the parent's right hand, which was watering the younger with the juice of a richer blessing. All these things are certainly contrary, if we think it was said of those who are born first of women from a man's seed: Every male that opens the womb. But since that decree holds something else within, therefore firstborn of this kind give way and lose their blessings. David, son of Jesse, not the first, or second, or third, but last of all, is anointed by the prophet, and, the most despised of all, is chosen for king. Nor does the decree of the law published about the firstborn favour the first or second against David, since it would surely have judged them the greatest if it had judged that their mothers' wombs were opened by them: when, then, or in what woman do we say this was fulfilled, which surely could not fail to be fulfilled? Who is she whose womb a child opens, not a husband? What virgin conceives who did not cease to be a virgin in order to conceive? Certainly not the one of whom Scripture says: Adam knew his wife, and she bore him a son (Gen. 4); but the one of whom the evangelist notes: And Joseph did not know her until she bore a son (Matt. 1). Therefore this was without doubt accomplished in Mary, whose womb no deflowerer of virginity opened, but the birth as it came forth; who as a virgin gave birth, who as a virgin conceived, who was made a mother before she was married. From her came forth that male who was truly to be called holy; and he, brought forth by birth according to the promise, opened the womb, not according to custom and common nature, by being conceived from a man's seed.

CHAP. VI. — But since we cannot quickly unfold the rich meanings of God, with the movements of the scriptures setting themselves against a single form in such numbers that it is easier to grow weary than to get through: for although all scripture is one path of all meanings, who will be able to run through it in human speech, not even if the Spirit were to attach angelic wings to the tongues of mortals? So it is fitting to return to our purpose, and not to set the sails of a small boat for the deep sea, lest boldness run into danger, but, as a comfort to our weakness, to sail within sight of the shore, so that if any fear arises there may at least be hope of easily reaching what is in view. We were saying that the holy Lord is the seed of the woman, because according to the flesh he had no human father, and that he was already hostile to the serpent, he whom the Spirit of God, not a material fluid, had begotten in the virgin's womb. Then what follows draws a greater result from the virgin's person: She will tread on your head (Gen. 3). Who doubts that no one apart from our Lord has trodden on the serpent's head? For he alone walked upon dragons and scorpions; he led captivity itself captive. And you will lie in wait for her heel: to whom else do we believe this refers? The heel is the farthest part of the footprint. And the Lord, after John's baptism, after a fast of forty days, when he is tempted by that same serpent, already victor over that third deceit, cries out: Get behind me, Satan (Matt. 4). What else is he commanding, but that, placed or thrown behind his back, [Satan] should watch his heel? I said this above, and the discourse itself has led us from there to this: that the inner man, when he thinks not in this world but above the world itself, seems to live with that Maker of things and his own Maker, as David says: Blessed are those who search out his testimonies (Ps. 11), so that to meditate on divine things is almost, if it may be said, to become God; that our Lord had already then revealed the mystery of our salvation; whence he says in the psalms: At the head of the book it is written of me (Ps. 39). The head of the book is the beginning of Genesis, since all Scripture is one book, and one God, of whom it is written; and so we see that the promise about him is at the head, and the head of our life is hope, and therefore the head of the book of life is the hope brought about through God. That he, I say, the Creator, as we have often said, when the world was already growing old, fulfilled what he had promised in the first age of the world. Hence the prophet says: Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me (Ps. 22). The rod is the mother of the Lord, from whom came forth this staff, to support the world now weary with age. That he, then, having descended into the virgin's womb (to retell the whole story of our redemption), made by birth, presented himself as man for man's sake, and made himself his creature, from being Creator. That he took the form of a servant, but emptied himself by the will of his power, not by the nature of his deity, through which he could not fail to be what he had been. That in return for saving miracles he earned curses. That he endured spittle, wounds, a crown of thorns, and finally the cross; that he went down into hell, that on the third day he rose again in the very body that had been fastened to the cross, that as man after death, the living God, he went up victorious to heaven, sits at the right hand of God, and will come in his own time to carry out the judgement: that he is celebrated by the Spirit of God through the mouths of his saints. To have thought on these things is to have lived; this thought is the food of the soul; to sink back or run back into these things is to be joined to the Lord, and to be humbled with him through them is to suffer with him, to die with him, and also to be raised with him. What shall I say of the resurrection itself, for which, though we are laughed at by the gentiles, we are not separated from Christ, even though many who call themselves Christians shut out the resurrection of the flesh? But let them be without a body, those to whom perhaps it is granted, if it may be said, to be presented to the Lord otherwise than as the Lord returned to the Father, as we believe and say.

CHAP. VII. — What, I say, is more joyful than this thought? What could be more uplifting than this? And this ought to cling more firmly in our minds: that at some time, when we have departed from here, we shall return to our bodies; and that the separation of soul and body in the meantime does not bring it about that we are nothing at all, but that we are re-formed better through the Spirit of God, since we have received that the Lord has already promised us this pledge here. And this body, which is perishable in its own nature, and weighed down by the guilt of the first transgression, and is carried along under the divine curse, will go to the earth (Gen. 3); and this, again, after long ages, that is, at the end of the ages, when only the smallest part of ash remains, or perhaps none at all, is to be renewed by that same earth which corrupts it to nothing (since the earth itself is to be freed from the slavery of corruption) into the entire solidity of its members, and into a state of beauty and comeliness. Whom would such a thought not delight, along with wonder? The remains, I say, of our bodies, either none or certainly very small, and however slight, yet foul, and never looked upon without the mind's horror, are to be joined together again into their own man, not so that one may be believed to be in Euphorbus, as Pythagoras falsely and madly claimed, but into one's own proper body and name, through bones and sinews, through veins, through all the vital parts, and indeed joint by joint. Nor is this hard to grasp, since the seeds of all crops and plants come back greater and more beautiful in their shoots than when they were sown in the earth by men or fell of their own accord. Who would not rejoice, so to speak, to be sown in the earth, which gives us back better than it received us, as the Apostle says: The resurrection of the dead: it is sown in corruption; it will rise in incorruption (1 Cor. 15)? What possession of present things can be compared with this hope? Or what else will there be that lifts us to contempt of death, than this meditation, unfolded by divine promises and the voices of the prophets? What such thing had Cleombrotus of Ambracia learned from the book in which Plato argues, he who did not fear to be his own murderer, and threw himself from a very high wall, since he held that there is no judgement after death, and thought that all souls after their bodies are carried equally to heaven without any distinction of merits? This all of them held so firmly as true, and one cloud of this error so wrapped all those wise men of the world, that even Socrates himself, so praiseworthy a teacher, as they think, killed himself privately as his own murderer, so as not to be put to death publicly. Far different was what the blessed Apostle had premeditated and thought out: he who had received what he taught not from men, but through the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ (Gal. 1), not sheltered in the dark shades of the wooded Academy, but enlightened by heavenly light; not taught in some elementary school among yawning little boys, but in the third heaven among shining angels; in contempt of the present life he cries out: For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain (Phil. 1). Certainly he does not seek a wall from which to throw himself to death, but Christ the Lord, through whom this mortal is to be swallowed up by immortality. For he understands that to die is gain for one whose future life is to be with Christ. But without the Lord it profits nothing, even if one gains the whole world, but is to suffer the loss of his own soul. The vessel of election, then, believed manfully that through Christ our Lord, from this earth, which never gives back what it receives without interest, but sometimes with less, often with greater increase, as thirtyfold and sixtyfold and a hundredfold, the Lord himself in the Gospel thus gathering the shoots he had planted; from which earth comes also the truth which Pilate did not know, which none of the princes of this world saw: For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Cor. 2); from this earth, I say, the Apostle says that he, transformed to the body of the Lord's brightness, will return in shining members: Wisdom also promising this through Solomon, when she says: The just will shine, and will run to and fro like sparks among the reeds (Wis. 3). And therefore he burst out confidently into this cry: For me to live is Christ (Phil. 1), in which, surely, merits that existed will live on; but those who were far off, as they did not know, so they will not be known. Now, if you agree, let us inquire what that saying of Solomon promised: The just will shine, and will run to and fro like sparks among the reeds. Why is it that those to whom the brightness of flames is granted are offered so lowly and mean a place to run in, so that by the contempt of the place they seem to diminish, who have grown in the light of their bodies? Why, I say, will they, compared to stars, flit through reed-beds, and in the form of starry brightness pass through the most wretched plants of the earth, when brightness is most unfittingly mixed with reed-beds, or reed-beds with brightness? Consider, I beg you, the words of the divine mystery, which has no care for reed-beds, just as it has none for oxen: or what are reed-beds doing in the resurrection, except that it labours to show us [ourselves] through the forms of all things, whether of cattle or of plants; and for this reason, as the Apostle says, all things were written for us (Rom. 4)? Understand that by the images of the reed-bed unbelieving and faithless men are shown, and their bodies, pleasing on the surface and inwardly empty of virtues, which, as soon as the spirit of vanity has puffed them up, imitate the hissing of the serpent, and, a brood of vipers, follow [...] sound offspring. Sparks, he says, among the reeds. Saints, then, among sinners, since not all flesh is the same flesh. Among the reeds, he says, that is, bodies empty of light, and about to burn with another's brightness, for whom the brightness of the saints will be a punishment: since God is a consuming fire, and the just will come into the image of the Godhead. For God made man; in his own image he made him (Gen. 1); and the Apostle testifies that he believes he will of necessity be like him. For if he was like God when he was made, he will also be like him when he rises again: since whatever in us now seems unlike the Maker has all been stamped on us by the vice of transgression; and the craftsman of lies disfigured the living form of truth with swelling needles, and inscribed his own depravity even on our members while he corrupted our minds; these things, wrongly added or taken away, will be washed out through the glory of the resurrection, and only that which reflects the Maker of things as in a mirror will shine forth: so that the falsifier may grieve that he has lost his work, and man may at last glory that he is whole. Yet not all, as we have already said, but only the just, will be in light. For we shall all rise again, but we shall not all be changed (1 Thess. 4); for the difference of merits will make the distinction of persons. For if even among the saints themselves there will be some difference according to their works, as the Apostle says: Star differs from star in brightness (1 Cor. 15), what difference shall we perceive in the case of the impious or of sinners, of whom some rise in judgement, others in the council of the saints? And if they are separated at the very time of the resurrection, what shall we say of their dress and form? This, it seems to me, will be procured not by any woven garment, nor by one worked from women's spinning, but by their own merits and prayers: as blessed John shows in the Revelation, who says he saw the saints clothed in fine linen (Rev. 19) clothed in fine linen. And lest perhaps we should look for a covering or threads under the fine linen, and suppose that something material, or corruptible and fleeting, is at work in heavenly places, he added: But the fine linen is the righteous deeds of the saints. Then, therefore, as I understand it, the things that are now hidden under the body will come to the surface of our body. Then to each one (wretch that I am!) his own conscience will become his garment. Then the things that each one has built upon that foundation, beside which no other can be laid (1 Cor. 3), will stand out, so that either he who set up things that will last receives a reward, or he who built things that will burn suffers loss. Now why should I recall what follows, which belongs wholly to the saints? Flesh without earth, a body without the sense of pain, a soul without fear, life without end, age without time, light without night, blessedness without end? I see man, and in man God: since God is all in all (1 Cor. 15). Whatever is now seen to be impossible for man [will] then be done through the munificence of the everlasting King: to veil and to unveil, to melt and to grow solid again, and [man] to become like him whom the solid and bodily mass of walls and doors did not feel as he entered to the disciples, and whom yet they all saw standing inside before them. And all that the Spirit of God cherished without this body, the body together with the Spirit of God will bring into being. Christianity cannot be sated with the delight of this knowledge. This is its rest, this its pleasure, this its joy, these its delights: to go in mind to the seat of God, and there to claim for itself a place and a share of that seat, not by its own presumption but by the promise of the Godhead. Nor does this seem hard to it, since it already knows that its own manhood is there in Christ the Lord. It claims for itself an equal right from its kinship with the flesh taken up by God: since we are of his flesh and of his bones. For he is the head of the body, the Church; he is the beginning of every principality and of the powers, as the Apostle proclaims: From whom the whole body, thus compacted and extended through joining, and bound together, grows into the increase of God (Col. 2). Why then should I speak of the judgement to come, and the day of the Lord, to be longed for by the pious and fled from by the impious; why of that flood of fire, not of waters, with the earth smoking, the sea fleeing, and the sky rolled up like a book? These things are grievous to the rich of the world, but to be awaited by the poor of Christ, for whom the Lord sighs in the psalm, saying: Because of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor, now I will arise (Ps. 12). What of that tribunal, immense with the majesty of the Judge, and to be revered for its twelve seats, and of the power so great given by the Son that in judging they have even the substances of angels made over to them, as if [they were] their creator, as the Apostle says: Do you not know that we shall judge angels too (1 Cor. 6)? And what will there be that is not believed to be handed over to those to whom even that spiritual nature of wickedness is to be subjected? What then will they do who now glory in honours, who through dreadful prefectures and fasces and consulships everlasting (as they think) strive to make themselves equal to God by robbery, not by nature? What will he do who joins house to house? who, throwing the city into turmoil and breaking all the boundaries that hemmed him in on every side, leaping over mountains, rivers and seas, wishes, so far as it rests with him, that the land which is common to all should be one estate, and, with insatiable greed overpassing the breadth of the immense globe, spreads himself out into the anxiety of Alexander of Macedon and the countless worlds of the Epicureans, and, having acquired by greed the narrow bounds of this world, credulous of another, is set on fire without weighing the capacity of his own body, thinking that he will suffer a loss of his rights if he does not put faith in his madness? What will those do who, like censors of morals, tear apart and harass the household of the Lord, living more carefully and more chastely, in clothes of humble colour, in dry sparingness of food, in the not idle sobriety of vigils, as if it were made delicate by softer clothing, or fattened on richer feasts, or yawning on warmer couches, not knowing that in the holy martyrs and confessors of God the pupil of his eye is struck? They will perish without doubt, all their thoughts will perish in that day: nor will Lucius Crassus defend them before that tribunal, or Mark Antony, or Tully, more eloquent than these: since then every tongue of the world will fall silent, and justice alone will be eloquent in her humble rustics, she who made the mouths of infants articulate, and loosed the tongues of the dumb into a new song, and in her mercy won for herself a heavenly harmony from her little sheep. To celebrate her glory, even if the efforts of men should cease, condemned stones are pointed to, to the confusion of the human race. But I have strayed from the subject I set myself, as if to rebuke the wickedness of mortals. And like a public accuser of one uniform evil, I have not spared worldly vices, while I pity certain people. Yet even if it were the time for judging, I would not dare to throw a stone at the adulterer; even if the authority of a purer conscience armed me for the judgement of an innocent man, I ought still to wait for the time, as the Apostle teaches, who did not take judgement away from the saints but put it off. For he says: Do not judge before the time (1 Cor. 4), hinting that that time of the resurrection is to be awaited, at which the flesh, restored to life through the glory of incorruption, will stand wonderful at the judgement, with steadfastness now abiding for eternity, when fear of falling will depart: it will not then tremble to pass sentence on another, when it has earned security about itself. But now all things are doubtful, all wavering, as the Apostle says: Considering yourself, lest you too be tempted (Gal. 6), you who, not knowing your own state, readily pass judgement on another's fall. What if you send confidence to the wretched, so that God may give it to the blessed? Let us rather praise the rewards of the saints, that is, true things, than be branded as improvident or untimely, either as to conscience or as to time.

CHAP. VIII. Let us return, then, to those most noble and most joyful thoughts of the saints: for nothing is more joyful than for a mortal to meditate on the inheritance promised to him. Let us set before our eyes that [day] of which we spoke, since it is safer to celebrate true things than to blame things to be pitied, although truly happy things cannot be told without the unhappiness of sinners. Let us see, then, as we determined, the saints of God flying everywhere with torches, and, with right hands flashing for vengeance, drawing two-edged swords. For this is the glory of the saints of God, this the warfare despised in this world, this the one torn apart by the tongues of all in their slanders. This will then be the fruit of our patience, this the reward of our endurance. These are the rewards for those blasphemed for the Name: to have subject to them every proud soul and every man who exalts himself; the once most powerful kings of the world, adored by the whole globe, to be set up in iron manacles and fetters, and their nobles, bearing the weight of huge chains on neck and shoulders, to be presented before the brightness of that august tribunal to those whom they once scorned, despised and mocked. For the lot is reversed: as this world belongs to the well-off, so [we must] believe the other will belong to the wretched. For woe to the rich, since they have received their reward; but to those rich to whom it will have to be said: I was hungry and you did not give me to eat; I was thirsty and you did not give me drink (Matt. 25). To those rich, that is, who would not make friends of the unrighteous mammon, who planned in their thoughts, when the harvest overflowed with which they refreshed no one, to build new storehouses for immense harvests, not knowing where they would eat tomorrow. Their soul was demanded of them at that time, though occupied in vain anxiety for a single night, since they did not cease to lay up treasure, nor fail to keep watch over buried wealth. Hence Lazarus the poor man, with that patriarch who lived as a stranger in the world, rejoices in his resting-place. But the rich man, on the contrary, burns in everlasting fires, and, stripped of all rank and substance, implores the divine help of the needy man he once despised, and longs to be touched even by the tip of the little finger of him whose want he would not relieve, amid his rich dishes and lavish banquets, even with the crumbs falling from the table. Since, then, the prescribed judgement is to be carried out through us, that is, through the saints, vengeance on the nations and the peoples has been given to us. When this is thought on, what mind is in us, what ardour of spirit, what desire for things to come, what contempt for things present, can more easily be felt than said. Or who is there who, hastening towards these things, does not desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ (Phil. 1)? Or what great thing is it if death is despised for such and so great goods, for which even this life is to be despised? Since whoever loses his life for these, saves it. But on the contrary whoever saves his life here will lose it. For since very many in this world are so set on fire in mind by ambition, as by the flames of the Furies, that they spare neither hoarded wealth nor inheritances, nor even their own children, whom, when accused of avarice, they are wont to put forward [as excuse], while they buy prefectures and consulships, offices which death takes away and a successor shuts out: what madness is it not rather to purchase, at every expense and at the loss of life itself, those things which make those advanced in them either secure of eternal life or glorious in the everlasting dignity of the judgement?

CHAP. IX. The time prompts, and the place itself suggests, nor does the subject seem foreign, since we have begun to treat of the merits of the saints, that we should wash away the blasphemies of a most unhappy unhappiness which seem to belong to this matter. For there have been those who chose to bite with slander rather than receive with veneration the outstanding and heavenly miracles worked through the relics of the saints, indeed almost in our own times, vomiting against the servants of God that ancient poison of Jewish unbelief which those men once poured out against the Lord himself with viperous tongues and deadly hissing, saying: By what power do you do this? and who gave you this power (Matt. 21)? For they recited to us, who were near by, what foolish unbelief was saying of the divine and most blessed Gervasius and Protasius, whom, while they schemed to take something from Pope Ambrose, they did not fear to violate with sacrilegious words, seeking out the reason for the miracles in this way: What is this, that because they are martyrs they have earned gifts of miracles? Why is what was granted them long ago exercised so late? Or if they did not show it at the time when they suffered, how have they worked it now? What is this that they seem to show only now? Or did Ambrose make them greater by revealing them than the honour of martyrdom did? Do you recognise, though in other words, that what we have reported of the Lord has been thus falsely heaped on the martyrs: By what power do you do this? and who gave you this power (Matt. 21)? A lukewarm consolation, as I judge, and born of envy, to ask whether what you see to be divine is divine, and to demand a reason when it is necessary to believe. And since the Apostle says: Love believes all things (1 Cor. 13), who doubts that those who have not given faith to such great miracles are without the love of God? And he denies faith who, like a tempter, asks: Whence this power? as if it were not manifest that the holy martyrs now work miracles in the spirit by the same power by which they formerly overcame their adversaries in the flesh and in their passion. Let us join battle against these (if it may be said) sons of the Jews, and as we lately overthrew their parent, that is, the Jew, who thought himself exceedingly wise in sacrifice, by the gift of the Godhead, so let us also destroy this brood of blasphemies under the Christian name, through him who said: I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the prudence of the prudent I will reject (1 Cor. 1): that we too may glory through the Lord in a double triumph, and they may recognise that the understanding of divine things is founded in the catholic faith, not in the wisdom of the world, as the Lord warns: Unless you believe, you will not understand (Isa. 7): so that it may be more evident both that the obscurities of unbelief lie open to the faithful, and that even the plain things of faith are not seen by the unfaithful. Perhaps, in your care and watchfulness and lively diligence, you may ask what that question was in which the Lord granted us a trophy over the false Israelite. I will relate it and not keep silent, since you love to have the page extended with such things. For although it may not seem fitting to insert other matters begun before the earlier ones are finished, yet for your sake I prefer to say some things even out of their order rather than pass over what has just now been granted me through your prayers. One of the enemies of the cross of Christ, among the intimates of God and indeed among the teachers, concerning that stumbling-block of his nation which they took up against our Lord, striking at the Lord with a spirit of blasphemy, brought forward examples from the Law. And as his father the murderer once, tempting the Lord on the pinnacle of the temple, wickedly proclaimed what had been promised about him in the Law, so this man, lest he should seem less learned in his perfidy, or his lie lie bare without greater authority, said: Our prophet Elisha does more miracles than your Lord Christ. For while you report as a great thing that Lazarus was called back into the light (John 11), what more can you say than that a dead man was raised by a living one? I bring forward what is reckoned true even by your own admission. For our Elisha (2 Kgs 13), when already dead, by contact with his bones, lifeless, gave life to a dead man (whom a crowd, fleeing the approach of raiders and abandoning the task of the last rites, had thrown down beside his body), and from cold bones and a bloodless body suffused another's corpse with vital warmth; nor did he give what he had, but granted to another what he himself did not then have. This, I believe, must seem to you greater than other miracles, that a dead man was sent back into the breath of life by a dead man, and that at the time when he himself was bound by the law of nature, he loosed the law of nature. If this surpasses all works, why is he not held superior, whom you too confess to be a prophet and a lord? Or if you know anything even like this, declare it, so that he may excel in honour who has been more excellent in the merit of miracles. Our leading men were stunned at these words, and returning no answer, nor bringing forward any weapon to strike back, they almost fell beneath the empty engine and useless battering-ram of their adversary: so much so that he who ought, as they say, to have been a fugitive from all, carried off even the glory of a victor without a contest. When this was reported to me, I groaned that there was such negligence in us that we cannot establish the truth, while others are able to drive home a lie in place of truth; and I asked the Lord, since nothing is ours, to supply arms to his own, so that the reproach of their sloth might be taken away. Give me, I said, that braggart who says: Our lips are our own, who is our Lord (Ps. 11)? I will surely bring it forward, through him who destroys the boastful tongue, so that they may understand that the servant is not to be made equal to the master, although the Jews themselves know that the ancient prophets performed no miracles by their own power. Indeed Elisha himself (2 Kgs 2), when he had inherited the spirit of his master, as though he had come somewhat elated by the reward of gifts, could nevertheless not divide the waters except by calling upon God. I confess that the power of the question now put forward was for a while such that the glory of our faith may be greater, if we crush the temptation even while we believe. What do you say, blasphemer of the Lord? Elisha, he says, himself dead, raised another dead man by the touch of his body. At this point fully, as in all things, the prophet's power rises up to its Lord's, [the power] which was in the Lord Jesus Christ, when your unbelief fortified his tomb with stones and soldiers besieged the stone, so, I believe, that his resurrection should not lack fitting witnesses. For you knew he would rise again, if you had been willing to believe; for suddenly, when the hinges of the underworld and of the earth were shaken, to the stupefaction of the soldiers and with the overthrow of the rocks, he raised not some other person but himself into the light. If these gifts had been Elisha's own, he would have preferred to give them to himself; nor could he provide to another what he himself lacked. Indeed, even your forefathers declared that this was greater, when they mocked the Lord on the cross, saying: He saved others, let him save himself; let him come down from the cross, and we believe him (Matt. 27). So we win by the verdict of your own people. Your people promised that they would believe if he had provided for himself what he was accustomed to provide for others. Why do you not believe what you do not deny to be more excellent? Certainly no one had this power. Indeed the Lord too says of his life: I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it up again (John 10). Review the proud images of your forefathers, and go over again the miracles of the patriarchs, and you will find who had such power. Why should I not believe that he can free my soul, who could free his own? As I was about to say more, recollection suggested that the volume was growing, and that therefore the course of this question must be called back, since that earlier one still stands at the door, to which its own space is equally due, still untouched, though with tighter reins. And truly much need not have been said on this part, lest he too should swell [with pride]: if indeed he should think he had brought forward something great, seeking victory by a lengthy disputation, whose pride, which abounds, not his wisdom, of which there was none in him, we have crushed.

CHAP. X.—Now that this Israelite has been dismissed, or else lest he boast that he made a fight of it (since what we have said we brought forward for the instruction of our own people rather than for a contest and clash with them, for he refuses to believe even when he is beaten), and lest we be judged to have shamelessly given what is holy to dogs, or to have scattered pearls before swine (Matt. 7), we must return to the point from which I strayed to this place, almost cutting off the paths of the argument; and the sheep of the house of Israel must be visited more carefully: since if the love of God is in us, who is weak, and I am not weak? who is made to stumble, and I do not burn (1 Cor. 11)? And they must rather be taught, so that they do not go so far as to speak blasphemies, if perhaps they either do not keep or do not understand what was prophesied. They ask whether it is divine power that has now begun to appear in the martyrs. Men of what law ask this? Of the Christian law, surely, which is so furnished with prophecies that nothing so new, so unexpected can befall in our times that a more chosen faith would not marvel at it, or a weaker one blaspheme it. All things up to the Lord the ancient prophets foretold. All things after the Lord that were lacking, the apostles prophesied: blessed Paul, through the freedom of the Holy Spirit, did not keep silent, saying: We know in part and we prophesy in part (2 Cor. 13): not that he does not know all things or does not prophesy all things, he in whom above all Christ speaks; but in part he prophesies of the whole, and in part he knows of the whole. He prophesies to us what he knows belongs to that time which was to come. What he prophesies, he prophesies indeed for an age to come. Yet he prophesies the whole, even if he prophesies in part. For he prophesies those things whose disclosure was needed by the part of that time which remains until the end. He prophesies in part, therefore, since in part it had already been prophesied: and so the prophet knew the things to come which he prophesied. The fragments of this prophecy the fullness of time, as he himself said, has done away with, in this way: When that which is perfect has come, that which is in part will be destroyed (ibid.): that is, when at the close of the world neither greater knowledge nor further prophecy is to be sought. Then, to show more plainly the force of this understanding, he added: We see now through a mirror in an enigma; but then face to face (ibid.). Meanwhile all things are in figure, and shadowed over with certain outlines of images, so that the weakness of our flesh and our earthly substance might stretch itself further towards the truth of spiritual things, so that that [truth], glimpsed faintly even through a mirror, might stir in it a desire for its beauty, and teach us how great it is in its own substance, since it appears so wonderful even in enigmas reflected by its light: and so we now behold the promises through a mirror, yet do not yet possess them on account of the merits of virtues: and we marvel at them in a still obscure light, we do not hold them as delivered. But then prophecy and knowledge will cease, when entry will have been made into the very power of all the promises which was being promised. Hence too prophecy is always obscure, because it is sung at one time and seen at another. What is said while it is not seen is not believed, as though it had not been foretold. Thus Isaiah, when he had been found worthy to recognise our redemption so long beforehand in the Virgin's womb, and pointed it out to the people as though already present, saying: Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel (Isa. 7), troubled both the present and the future generation of unbelieving Israelites. For those of old killed their prophet, because they did not see what he showed; and these killed the one prophesied to them, because they did not receive the prophecy. We must take care that this does not befall us too, if our age blasphemes those whom an earlier age persecuted. And since, as we have said, what had been foretold has come, there is nothing to come which was not foretold before, as the Lord himself says: Behold, I have foretold all things to you (Mark 13). Let us rather see whether these things, which are now represented to our eyes as fulfilled, are shown at some time to have been poured into the ears of our forefathers. Let us see whether one and the same Spirit works all these things (1 Cor. 12). Whether, finally, not even an angel from heaven preaches a gospel other than what has been preached to us: although they themselves, through the torments of the demons, bear witness to what are the powers of the Lord, since Satan does not cast out Satan: because the sameness of wickedness, fused naturally into an undivided fellowship, fears no loss of itself from the addition of what is like it, but gains increase. For a confederacy of depraved spirits and viperous iniquity had massed many into the form of one legion; nor did their multitude harm them, which, just as it gained a wretched strength from associated weakness, so dreaded falling, by being divided with permission, into the emptiness of a void substance.

CHAP. XI.—But having let go this part of the argument for the time being, let us prove, as we proposed, that the things we marvel at in the churches of the Lord and the cemeteries of the saints are to be believed to be done by divine power, if they have been prophesied. And in this matter, so hard and difficult and not treated by anyone before, we ought to consult the Lord, if we did not fear to be rejected for our boldness, since merit is lacking: for no one apart from him will be able to explain what is his. Indeed it is a wonder whence the wretched have such confidence, whence so friendly a familiarity in addressing the Lord, that we dare to burst out with this cry: Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth (Song 1). Who has conceived so great a wish? Who, a careless appraiser of himself, has sighed out such great desires, that he longs to touch his very mouth face to face? Would that he might at least deem us worthy of the kiss of those whom he himself deigned to kiss: so that, standing last in the second and third ranks, we might be found worthy to draw some knowledge in part from the lips of those who learned the whole fullness of wisdom from the mouth of the Lord himself. And yet, even if we were propped up by the privileges of great merits, there were set in examples, like certain deep foundations of modesty laid down again, lest the presumption of disordered levity dare anything unseemly. What more chosen than blessed Peter? What more uplifted to hope? What freer in faith, he whom the Lord promised to kiss with the kiss of his mouth, saying: To you I will give the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and this: Upon this rock I will build my Church (Matt. 16). Yet he, bowing himself under a certain weight of modesty, lowered the confidence which, more exalted, he had from merit, and became more modest in asking, when at the Lord's supper he did not himself ask who was to betray the Lord, but humbly and bashfully sought the Lord's kiss through another's mouth: which he [did], although he had confidence with the Lord, such that he would presume on it unshaken even as a man, as there, when he dares to ask the Lord walking on the sea that the backs of the waters, made solid under his steps, might bear him up likewise; [here he was] somewhat more distrustful of himself, but more prudent for us, before whom by his act he set forms to imitate, as in a mirror. If he cautiously explores the Lord's foreknowledge through an envoy, what is worthier than this teaching? What subtler than this art of consulting, which we ought to practise, who, since we have the confidence of no merit, ought at least to have the modesty of the example, imitating blessed Peter at least in this part, who showed not only with what humility, but also by what means we may arrive at what we desire. Let us seek the solution of this question from him whom he himself did not blush to ask. From him, I say, who, reclining on the very breast of the Lord, as upon the ark of the New and Old Testament, not only came as a diligent inquirer to the forecourt of some divine oracles, but entered as an intimate priest the very inner sanctuary of the secret dispensation; and so he alone saw the Word in the beginning, when to him, like the outer altar of the most holy temple, so the inner was committed to be measured. May he himself lead us, concerning that book which he wept over as closed with seven seals and rejoiced over when it was opened, not through some false figure, but through open doors, into his breast of truth.

CHAP. XII.—But lest we linger while he is being consulted, he anticipates those who inquire by the short way of foreknowledge: what he saw would at some time be a fearful thing to our minds, he illuminates. He even gives answers from Patmos, as though questioned. From that place, that is, where, no stranger, he entered the secrets of heaven closed to Caesar, and, driven from the company of men, came to know the mysteries of angels. For he says: I saw under the altar of God the souls of the slain martyrs on account of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus, which they held; and to each of them was given a robe; and they cried with a loud voice, saying: How long, O Lord, holy and true, do you not avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth? And to each of them was given a white robe, and they were told to rest yet a little while, until the number of their fellow servants and brothers should be completed, who would be killed afterwards after their example (Rev. 6). O Apocalypse truly divine, opened to so great an apostle at the very time of his confession, deservedly, so that they might be hardened the more to endurance when the merits of those who had suffered were shown to them! We must not then go astray through the leaves of the Sibyls, whose pages, as they wrestled with the evil spirits of an uncertain world, so their places were tossed by the winds of this air. See, most plainly the apostle sets out what he held, and brings light to a most obscure question. He had perceived that these things would one day have to be said, which now a more sinister tongue, its words softened by art as if with oil, hurls to the ruin of its hearers and its own. And therefore, he says, I saw under the altar of God the souls of the slain martyrs. About the faith of the witness no one has any doubt: let the testimony be examined; let the understanding of the answer waver, not the authority of the speaker.

CHAP. XIII. — And first we must notice that the apostle testifies that he saw the souls of the slain martyrs, so that no one, when we begin to discuss their gifts, may say that what the souls are shown to have been granted even now is to be bestowed on the martyrs only after the resurrection. This is all the more so since what supports us is that they complain about the delay of the judgement, a delay which only one who is still to rise accuses, not one who has already risen: for it is one thing to ask that you may hold, another to hold already. Robes, moreover, are given to the army of the martyrs, and, as if ungrateful for so great a generosity, it assails heaven with great reproach over the slowness of vengeance. It reproaches [God] with words of no light weight, saying: How long, O Lord? That is to say: how long will you not avenge those whom you ought to have avenged at once? How long, O Lord? That is to say: are you putting us off beyond the end of the ages? For we have already come to the very end, and you say nothing of our vengeance. For they add what they say so wonderfully: Do you not avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth? So [it would] not [be] 'how long', if those mortals who persecuted the servants of the Lord with club, stone, hook, scourges, lead, iron, beasts and fire are still living on the earth. For 'how long' is a charge of a lengthier span of time, so that either 'how long' would be without end, and the persecutors still linger in the flesh, or they have departed this life, even if they dwell on the earth, if 'how long' does not deceive. But nothing false is put forward by the witnesses of truth; and therefore it is the interpretation that must be sought rather than the truthfulness, which is not shut out by a somewhat obscure way of speaking, but veiled. When, therefore, they say: How long, O Lord, holy and true, do you not avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth, they do not desire the blood and death of those mortals who once raged against them either in popular riot, or, backed by tribunals, pronounced capital sentences, on the ground that these still dwell on the earth; nor is it right that the dead should be accused, who, while they lived, were defended by these words: Do not lay this sin against them, for they do not know what they are doing (Acts 7). But if amid the torments of their sufferings and the bitter labours of death they pleaded so lovingly for the unjust, for the impious, for the bloodthirsty, for the blasphemers; if, finally, at the very time when the sense of their anguish could have roused those suffering the extremes to cursing, prayer was poured out for man, who does not understand that it was not the minds of the martyrs but the persons of the persecutors that were marked out, and that those are attacked who must be believed to have still dwelt on the earth at that time, whom ignorance indeed does not defend, and not those who have already ceased to dwell on the earth by the condition of their natural substance, and were long ago excused by the martyrs themselves on the ground of ignorance? Who these are we are not ignorant. Without doubt they are the spiritual forces of wickedness and the power of darkness, which both still dwell on the earth and sinned against the servants of God not in ignorance. For since they themselves said to the Lord: Why have you come before the time to torment us (Matt. 8)? how could they not know his servants, whom they would not even have persecuted had they not known them to be his servants? Therefore when they persecuted, they knew whom they were trying to drag away from their Lord by torments. And hence, since the blessed martyrs intercede for men and defend them with the excuse of ignorance, it follows that those who knew are held in the guilt, those who spread the very darkness of ignorance over men, whose fury even excuses human impieties: and we can call them none other than those who are not friends even to their own, since they do not allow them to be what is good; and they are enemies also to the servants of God, since they persecute them, not knowing what is good.

CHAP. XIV. — After the complaint of these holy souls, let us look at what follows: And white robes were given to each of them. What is this, that they are clothed again? For earlier, as it is written, they obtained garments from God; and now they are presented with clothing by a twofold generosity. Since these garments are certainly spiritual, we cannot fear that those which were given earlier are seen to be outside; nor indeed did any complaint arise [on that score]. Therefore, since the difference of these garments and their meaning is not without mystery, we must understand the varieties of gifts and the riches of operations, since one and the same Spirit supplies them. So they receive garments first, when they laid down their bodies through confession: so that, I believe, they might be found clothed, not naked. Again they receive other garments after their appeal, or rather after the change of so long a patience and endurance. And when they receive these, who does not understand that, as they are clothed in a new garment, so they are filled with the power by which they now shine forth and appear? But if they had asked for one thing and received another, they would either have rejected the gifts or, mocked, sought for more. But since it is not God's way to mock those to whom he has promised great things, and these do not complain after the second bounty, do we doubt that the appearances which were given to those asking for vengeance pertain to the consolation of their complaints? And if to consolation, what greater consolation could be found than this power, which persecutes the demons, that is, their own enemies? For if we compare these robes to the appearance of our clothes, let us also look for some others, so that they may not lack [them] when these are laid away. But this, which first comes to mind, is ridiculous, because it departs from the true and necessary interpretation. The complaint arose from the delay of vengeance. Indeed at the end of the times, that is, of ours, for upon us the ends of the ages have come, so that it is thought a delay, to dispel this the souls are clothed with robes, so that they might not be thought altogether naked, without greater protection. For the condition of souls stripped of the body is one thing, that of men still living in the flesh another. For us the fleeces of sheep and the work of women provide clothing; for them their merits make a garment. So when, after their complaint, the souls of the martyrs are wrapped in robes, they are presented with divine protection, with which that vessel of election also longed to be clothed over; and Adam, when he had lost this garment, was found naked even in paradise. Finally, the effect shows what we ought to understand by the robes. If we believe that the martyrs asked for vengeance, then we believe that they received something meanwhile for their consolation. If the complaint was calmed because of the robes, as by some distributions of clothes, who did not earn these even with the first gifts? But since, as I said, the varieties of powers with which illustrious souls are divinely furnished are signified by the robes, therefore after the second bounty, according to the form of their request against those persecutors who dwell on the earth, let them show what they are seen to have obtained, and what they will still have: while with like persecution they kill their fellow servants, until the predestined number of witnesses is filled up. Here this too must not be taken idly, that this cry of the martyrs came between two times of persecution, so as to mark out as blasphemers those who wonder that in our time they have obtained something new. For since we see that there were cruel persecutions, and believe that there will be [more] to come, this middle time, in which the martyrs who went before are rewarded, is ours. And therefore they are now at work, not by merit, which they always had, but by power, which they have recently gained.

CHAP. XV. — Perhaps someone may be troubled why they are told to wait, if the power has already broken forth which brings judgement on the demons to the ripeness of punishment, [and yet] they are told to await the resurrection. But this glory had been promised them also in the songs of David in these words: They shall rejoice in their beds (Ps. 149). While they are buried, then, they will rejoice. He put beds for tombs, from which they are also to rise when they are roused by the voice of the archangel and the trumpet of God (1 Thess. 4). So the places in which they now rest are truly called beds. Even if they will rejoice in their chambers, this was to happen first, namely when they rose from their tombs. And this has been so fulfilled that we see them without doubt rejoicing in their beds. For what other such gladness could enter their souls than when, before their very beds, that is, as we said, the tombs of the saints, their enemies, whom they once believed they had killed, confess, not without bitterness of torments, that they both live and take vengeance? This is what these robes, which a special bounty repeated, have conferred on them; through them those who were not named are invoked, those who were unknown are celebrated, and those who were not seen appear. These robes, as we said, they did not have until now, but now have begun to have. In this form that woman in Solomon is praised who makes double garments for her husband: one in the patience of suffering, the other in the power of vengeance. So it is holy and godly for us to read [it]: otherwise we ought not even to speak, lest either our unbelief or our ignorance sink into the darkness of paganism by blasphemous disputation, since prophecy went before for this reason, to bring light to those to come. Now it remains that the things we have proved to have been promised must be believed to happen by divine power, and not so much promised as also requested. And if they were both requested and granted to none but those who asked, what wonder is it if they do not hide either what they had asked for, or what they rejoice to have received beforehand? They exact punishment from those who dwell on the earth: those whom the accusation takes in, the power attacks. For those dwell on the earth who possess the minds of men who possess earthly things: and when the martyrs demand them for punishment, they also pray for those whom they had possessed. Finally, they so carry out their very desires as to shut them out of their earthly dwelling, that is, out of the possessed earthly men. Or do people cavil at why the demons are tormented, and do we side with the enemies? The martyrs rise up against them with an almost hostile indignation, and complain that they are tolerated through so long a span of ages: and we pretend to wonder what this is, as if they ought not, at least in our time, to pay what they have deserved since Adam. And as to the fact that this miracle is seen to have first arisen at Milan, or to have been granted to the good Ambrose, who does not see that our faith has been approved by divine testimonies because of the faithlessness of the Arians? For when the catholic faith in Italy had endured an intolerable tyranny under Auxentius, at length, the Lord granting its old freedom, it breathed again, even though already at the time when the aforesaid Ambrose was put in his place; yet to this very man, for the confusion of the adversaries and, of course, for our hope, all the glory of the heavenly ones, and all the martyrs too, agreed, who, though they had long had the time for appearing, were seeking a man to whom they might reveal themselves; surely one to whom they might be revealed under that faith which had made the martyrdoms. So to Ambrose was granted what was denied to Auxentius, since what Auxentius blasphemed, Ambrose preached. But although this power of the martyrs was to go through all the provinces (for it is to be granted to all, not to Ambrose alone, without respect of persons), yet it necessarily went forth first in Italy, over which the Arian unbelief had ruled. For signs are given not to believers but to unbelievers (1 Cor. 14). For those who ask a sign of the Lord are unbelievers: the scribes ask, the Pharisees ask; the apostles are silent, and believe, and follow. And therefore it is not to be wondered at that the divine power works through the tombs of the saints, since the heretical mind could not be cured by its own remedies, so that at least at last it might follow the bishop with whom it had seen that even the martyrs, by the very revelation of their powers, deigned to be in communion.

CHAP. XVI. — Now let us return to the meditation of the perfect man, from which this heap grew up before its measure was filled. See, this discussion is about those very meditations of which David says: For blessed is he who will meditate on the law of the Lord day and night (Ps. 1). And indeed it is difficult, once one has entered the forest of the law, to separate the material of individual questions, since one touches another, as if by little branches, so closely through the fellowship of precept that it cannot unfold what it has begun without starting on another. See how fine it is for that man of ours to know these very things: to be the only one not astonished at such things, while he alone is not moved, as the rest are, as if by things that happen by chance; to distinguish the kinds of workings. And since even the demons work, [it is fine] to understand their natures, which are true and which false; and to know [this] is not to be deceived, not to go astray, not to assign to the enemy what is God's, nor to award to God what belongs to the demons; to know the times, to recognise the signs, to have the will of the Lord known; and to venerate some wonders of God with thanksgiving, and to shun others with fitting execration. Even men of the world have praised such a man, as Virgil says: Happy he who was able to know the causes of things. A good sentiment, if he had come to it by its proper road; but it appears that he did not know what he praises: leaving out what comes first, he celebrated what comes second. For by a reversed order he also overturns the duty of the wise man: since it is not the causes of things but the Creator of things that is to be sought, through whom, if we have learned of him, we shall enter into the causes of things. But if he is left out, how shall we be able to have the causes of things known, when we must first ask who made these things, and then why he made them? But once the author of things is found, we shall find the causes of things too. This he so far failed to see that he proclaimed as holding the first place the man who could know the causes of things, and, as he adds, the one who worshipped the gods second, as performing a lesser work; so that anyone may recognise that those were not the creators of things from whom the knowledge of things is distinguished as something foreign, and that they ought not to be worshipped if they cannot provide these things that are praised as first. For they do not know the things of which they were not the makers. Indeed, taking the discovery of these away from their gods, they assign it to human talent, namely to those who excel in wisdom, because they do not worship idols; so that man is now more powerful than their gods, if by loftier thought he has arrived at these things of which their gods are ignorant. And he directed that the gods be worshipped by those who through sheer stupidity cannot find the causes of things, and whose hearts, to use his own words, cold blood encloses. Furthermore, our man knows that to worship God is the chief wisdom, and he has the causes of things discovered; he does not seek to stand out by the Syracusan method of a worldly wise man, but by the teaching of him whom he worships, whom he sought before the causes of things: since the Founder of things comes before the things themselves; who has told him what things were to come at what times, whose disposition no one has known without him who disposed it: since no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God. But we, as the Apostle says, have not received the spirit of this world, but the Spirit which is from God (1 Cor. 2); and therefore we are skilled in his things, not taught by the words of human wisdom, but by the Spirit of God and by his condescension poured out upon us. This is that folly of worldly men, this the wisdom of the called: to think always in the heart: What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me (Ps. 116)? To have him always in the mouth, since he is the Word; to hunger for him, since he is bread; to be drunk with his Spirit and go out of one's mind, since he is the cup of the New Testament, and the wine from the vine which he had earlier brought over from Egypt, which vine was the people of Israel: whose are the fathers, from whom the Lord Jesus Christ came according to the flesh. To speak of him at all times, since his Spirit has brought us new tongues. And what are these new tongues, if not these: to be in the world and not to have talk of the world; to speak to the people in other tongues than the people has been accustomed to speak with itself? Besides, this too is to speak in other tongues: that one who used to confess many gods confesses one God, and in our faith speaks with new tongues of him as one, and professes and believes the Trinity. To love him too, because he intercedes for us; to fear him, because the Father has given all judgement to the Son; to adore him at every moment, to ask of him what is necessary for us and pleasing to him, who wishes to be asked by us for himself, so much so that he shows these words to the one who asks; who, a thing that is new among us, alone loves those who ask of him; who also alone, which is wonderful, is angry unless he is asked. For it is unbelief to have presumed nothing of God. He believes him able to do nothing who does not ask for what he judges him able to do. This, dearest son, is that narrow way, this that eye of the needle through which those laden with packs do not enter, nor animals assigned to burdens; since the narrow and small entrances not only do not admit these shapeless beasts with their loads, but even frustrate the very gaze of our eyes if it is drawn in many directions. Hence the Lord too says through the prophet: Be still and see (Ps. 46); and when will it be possible to enter what, amid the occupations of the world, has not yet even begun to be found?

CHAP. XVII. — We have filled out the questions proposed with their divisions, by showing the outer man and the inner man, when we showed what life is holy, in what activity it is set, by what pursuit it is held, by what substance it is nourished; and we have brought its whole course briefly to the end, though by leaps, if one may say so, rather than by steps, in our haste. Now hear the reason why it is not seen also by the men of this world, since my wordiness delights you, which you judge too leniently while you attend more studiously to divine things. When he who first brought in upon us the seed of death had subjugated this world, that is, the passion of man, by conquering man, and had taken his kingdom, its king now captured, under his feet and into his dominion, and was using everything that is in the world as his own property and the spoils of his victory: lest man should at some time seek the wisdom he had lost, or the testament of life owed to him, he so tainted everything with all the juices of his art that he both clothed folly in the colour of wisdom and shaded death with the enticements of a counterfeit life, so that those who did not perceive the better things set against them would not flee the evil. In short, from that time the human race has walked thus everywhere: folly is held for wisdom, as the Psalmist says: For the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the wicked man is blessed (Ps. 10). Then that is thought to be life which is death, and evils deceive under the appearance of good, when, to the deception of the understanding, the excellence of all good things is covered over by guile. For riches are loved which will not follow after a man's death. The honour of the fasces, which fades away through a successor, is canvassed for; to have done injury is excellence; to possess what belongs to others is power; to circumvent the innocent is shrewdness; not to know Christ is wisdom; to shudder at the prophet is eloquence: so full is everything of errors, so, as darkness falls on the minds of men, one rushing against another, is the world wrapped up, and truth is obscured to the point that to have lain in the lap of death is called blessedness. When that God, who always thinks of us and of our affairs, saw that through the wisdom of the world, in which the world had found for itself accomplices and falsifiers, his own wisdom had become deserted, it pleased him in turn, against the cunning of the old trickster, to use the innumerable riches of his wisdom, and the depth of knowledge which no one will be able to search out as it is, and to veil his wisdom with folly, and to hide his life in a certain obscurity of death, so that he who in this world had fled the reputation of folly could not arrive at wisdom, and he who had not had contempt of death would not approach his life. For thus he sent the Son, our Saviour, into man, that is, he clothed his Wisdom in flesh, which is folly; he made his way the suffering of the cross, which is death. Thus he destroyed adversity by its opposite, and by workings of his ingenuity unlike [those used] before the ages he shattered the engines of that artificer, so that by certain saving traces, as it were, his deadly brands, though impressed, were wiped out. But unless we desire this pursuit, since what is foolish of God is wiser than men (1 Cor. 1), we shall not hold his wisdom. And unless we love this death, which is the cross, since what is weak of God is stronger than men, we shall not be able to enter his life. What then follows, except that, leaving behind both the wisdom and the life of the world, we should suffer ourselves to be held fools, and always wish to die with the Lord? so that in the hope of his coming, which will be the revelation of both things, we may deserve to have some share. For then, all veils being torn away, all things will be seen each such as they are: that is, worldly folly will stand stripped of the wrappings of false wisdom, and death, uncovered from the veil of a counterfeit blessedness, its mouth always gaping and its throat open to the depths, will be betrayed as the enemy of living things. Then too the heavenly wisdom, which in worldly terms is called folly, will enter, the depth of the knowledge of God being set before [us], without the labour of any night-study, and true life will shine, obscured by no darkness of death, through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honour for ages of ages. Amen.

CHAPTER XVIII. — You see, my son, with what sickness the mind of the suspect labours that does not think on these things. I have applied soothing care to my poor body; if I neglected it, the soul would be stronger, for it is weakened when the outer [man] is strengthened. But may the frequency of your prayers heal this soul I have spoken of, corrupted by the disease of folly; for your soul, untainted by the shameful deeds of the world, is able to help others. For a sick man cannot apply the remedy of his own health to those pierced through by sickness, and one panting at the depth of his own wounds does not heal the wounds of others. Let him who is sound surely care for the sick; one who has eyes does not lead the blind over cliffs. So you, as one who is wise, entreat the Lord that I may become wise in what I have not been wise, and by your prayers, or by some remedies, have me healed. Someone may reproach me that I advanced so far into a delightful disputation that I lost the awareness of my own deserts, or that I, an unworthy disputer of such matters, suddenly mounted the narrow chair of Moses. But truly I did this out of love for you, not by usurpation of my own. For I had read what was said to the sinner, that he should not dare to recount the righteous deeds of the Lord with his mouth. But if, against the prohibition, I have presumed for love of you, your kindness will deign to make amends for it in this: that you do not so readily bring out to the public these little letters, which have not been fully corrected (as appears from the very characters in which they are written); and though I could not be as modest on my own behalf as I ought, let at least your restraint spare my modesty. And since they have it from me that they are badly written, let them have it from you that they are kept hidden. Farewell, and love us in the Lord, in whom you are loved by us.
